articles.title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
articles.content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second. The sermon matters enormously. But we’re learning that the sermon alone cannot do the heavy lifting of solving the Bible literacy crisis. It’s a passive learning environment, a one-way communication. Imagine if your local public school believed passively listening to a lecture was the only way to form students into contributing citizens. Why does the local church think people comprehensively learn the Bible in such settings? Imagine also if your local public school recommended peer-led discussion groups as a primary vehicle for educating students. Imagine if the time spent in these groups was used to reflect for 30 minutes or so on what was taught in a lecture several days before: Mrs. Harker lectures on the quadratic equation for 30 minutes on Monday; students discuss how to apply the quadratic equation to their lives for 30 minutes on Wednesday. Who’s passing an algebra exam? Yet, 95 percent of pastors surveyed responded that discipleship isn’t completed in a program but in a relationship. Hence, the ubiquity of the community-group model in evangelical churches. We Know What to Do The wildest part of this disconnect about how to teach what’s good in a way that sticks is that we know the answer. The answer isn’t a new thing but an old thing recently forgotten. The church must return to its roots as the solver of illiteracy, both within its walls and also without. Education pastors can be tempted to dabble, trying one thing or another to see what their church members might find interesting, buying the latest study from a Christian publisher on the assumption it’s good. The idea that there are well-attested best practices for Christian education seems to have gotten lost. Just like a healthy local school, churches need to reclaim active, dedicated learning environments—spaces designated explicitly for the purpose of teaching the Bible. They need to think like educators: What is the scope and sequence for what we’ll teach? And they need to ask a better question than “What do my congregants want to learn?” I didn’t want to learn grammar, but thank goodness, Mrs. Wagner knew I needed it and taught it to me anyway. Her evident enthusiasm for the topic fascinated me. What was I missing that she knew? I learned grammar in a dialogic space taught by a subject-matter expert with an evident love for her subject. That love was contagious. Imagine if the church taught people the Bible like Mrs. Wagner taught grammar. It might become the classic of classics that every Christian actually wants to read. Christians possess the most beautiful and compelling book of all. Because a book forms the foundation of our faith, Christians have always been invested in solving illiteracy. We’ve striven to train people to read because reading is essential to the promulgation of our faith. The roots of public education and university systems lie in Christian efforts to grow literacy. The availability of vernacular translations of the Bible is the result of a concern for readability for all. Sunday school began in the late 1700s as an effort to educate children who worked in factories prior to child labor laws, seizing their one day off work as a literacy opportunity. Christians have been literacy champions in previous dark ages—and Christians can be again. Don’t Look Away In the first article I ever wrote for The Gospel Coalition back in 2012, I considered the Bible literacy crisis: “Why does biblical ignorance continue to dog the church, despite the good intentions of leadership to obey the Great Command to make disciples? I believe the answer lies in our definition of a disciple. A disciple is, literally, a learner—one who follows another’s teaching.” Fourteen years later, I’m still asking church leaders to remember to teach learners as the most basic function of discipleship, and to do so with proven tools. Don’t look away from the problem. Don’t tell yourself it’s the problem of the church down the road. In a cultural literacy freefall, all churches will feel the negative effects in Bible liter
articles.content_zh:
1900年11月,马克·吐温向康涅狄格韦斯利安大学的学生发表了题为“文学失踪”的演讲。 他对他们说:「我不相信你们谁读过失乐园, 这是你想要信任的东西。 这是.
经典的定义——人人都想读,没有人想读。” Twain指出,现在我们目睹的文盲岩崩是雪崩的开始。 我们在智能手机和社交媒体时代所看到的统计数据证明了我们已经消退的识字率: 2003年,15岁以上的美国人平均每天读21.9分钟。
至2010年,该数字已降至18.3分钟,2025年,该数字已降至每天16.2分钟. 想象一下ChatGPT在接下来的几年里会如何进一步切断这个数字. 美国正在迅速进入一个 后文化的现实, 一种新的黑暗时代, 在其中,我们消耗信息 在图像和声音叮咬, 这一切都被其他人预知。
考虑一下对一种信仰体系的影响,这种信仰体系从一代传到另一代都与一本书有关。 基督教识字危机 生活之路研究的一项新的调查 将基督教对圣经的承诺 和对圣经的了解 之间的裂痕推向了严峻的解脱
在一个典型的月份里参加教堂的基督教徒超过2000人被调查了八类圣经知识:主要人物,经文,活动,圣经的分裂等等. 研究人员围绕什么是通常众所周知的而不是模糊的问题。 3个受访者中有2个得分低于60分,成绩不及格.
百分之五十五无法正确命名以色列第一任国王. 只有11%可以正确订购四大旧约事件,只有27%可以正确订购四大新约事件. 44%的人未能将马克的书确定为属于福音书.
3个受访者中有2个错误地认为赫泽基亚是一本圣经的书,44%的人也认为托马斯福音书也是. 基督教徒已屈服于文化的普遍识字危机。 “信奉天经的人”不读。 圣经本身,是所有经典的经典,显然已经成为每个基督徒都想阅读的书,很少有基督徒想阅读.
如果我们真的读到来维持我们的信仰,我们更可能阅读有关圣经的书籍,而不是圣经本身. 我们或许可以使用布道、播客, 或利用奉献资源,
散会失败 我认为这些结果表明门徒战略失败, 我们不能把自己所不知道的东西传给别人。 如果教会不能教别人观察耶稣的旨意, 数字显示我们连基本知识都没有教过。
如果教会是一所负责教授基本数学和阅读的当地公立学校,我们就会得到不及格的分数,并面临资金制裁. " 书人 " 不读。 然而,根据2024年对2,620名新教牧师进行的生活道研究调查,52%的人对其教会中的门徒身份和精神形成状况感到满意.
29%的人报告说,他们定期评估其教会中的门徒进步。
当被问及他们在门徒中的首要地位时,人数最多的回答是“以圣经知识为中心”。 在回答“你的教堂对门徒具体使用什么方法并鼓励成年人在会堂中的精神发展? ” 89%的人回答布道,这是最高的回答,有20点的差距,成人星期日学校排在第二位。
讲道很重要。 但我们知道, 单靠布道并不能解决圣经的识字危机。 这是被动的学习环境, 想象一下,如果你的当地公立学校认为被动地听一个讲座是组织学生为公民作出贡献的唯一办法。
为什么当地教会认为人们在这样的环境下全面学习圣经? 也想象一下当地公立学校是否推荐由同行领导的讨论小组作为教育学生的主要工具。 想象一下,如果在这些团体中花费的时间被用来反思几天前在一次讲座中教授的内容:
周一哈克关于四极方程式的讲座30分钟;学生周三讨论如何将四极方程式应用于他们的生活30分钟. 谁要通过代数考试? 但95%的受访牧师回应说, 因此,福音教会中普遍存在社区团体模式。
如何教善知识, 也就是我们知道答案。 答案并不是新事物, 教会必须恢复其根源,作为解决文盲问题的手段,无论是在其城墙内还是在城外。
教育牧师们可能会被诱骗, 尝试着看他们的教会成员会发现什么有趣的东西, 基督教教育方面有经过充分验证的最佳做法的想法似乎已经丧失。
正如当地一所健康的学校一样,教会需要恢复积极、专注的学习环境——明确指定用于教授圣经的空间。 他们需要像教育家一样思考: 我们将教授什么? 他们需要问一个比“我的同志们想要学习什么”更好的问题。 我不想学习语法,
瓦格纳知道我需要它 并且教给我 她对这个话题的明显热情让我着迷. 我错过了什么 她知道? 我在一个对话空间中学习了语法, 教授的是一位主题专家, 明显热爱她的主题。 那爱是传染性的。 想象一下如果教会像瓦格纳夫人那样教人圣经,教人文法.
这可能会成为每个基督教徒真正想要阅读的经典. 基督徒拥有最美丽最有说服力的书 因为一本书构成了我们信仰的基础,所以基督徒总是被投入解决文盲问题. 我们努力训练人们阅读,
公共教育和大学制度的根源在于基督教努力提高识字率。 圣经的方言译本的可用性是关注全民可读性的结果. 星期天学校于1700年代后期开始,以努力教育在童工法之前在工厂工作的儿童,抓住他们一天的休息时间作为识字的机会.
基督徒在黑暗时代是识字的冠军, 不要走开 我在2012年为福音联盟撰写的首篇文章中,认为圣经的识字危机是:"尽管领导者有服从大命令让门徒成为门徒的好意,但圣经的无知为何仍然在坚持教会?
我相信答案就在我们对门徒的定义上 从字面上讲,一个弟子是一个学习者——一个听从他人教导的人。 十四年后, 我仍然要求教会领袖们记住, 教导学习者, 不要忽略问题。 不要告诉自己,这是教堂在路上的问题。
所有教会都会在圣经里感受到负面影响

articles.title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
articles.summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
articles.summary_zh: 兰登·霍布森(Landon Hobson)是宇宙公司(Cosmos Corporation)的首席执行官,是圣路易斯以外的一家家庭企业,在70个国家销售宠物护理和家庭清洁产品. 凭借神学和经济学的学位,兰登从未预期会经营25万平方英尺的制造厂——直到他的岳父要求他接管公司,他觉得上帝一直在为他做好完全这样的准备. Landon描述了他的信仰如何塑造宇宙文化:为雇员想要追求的任何学位提供学费支持,一个支付人们阅读费的“更好的书社”,每年5个付费的任务日,以及“愿意为你背后的人煮咖啡”的核心价值。 他直言不讳地说, 连锁供应中断、销售量下降、以及他所关心的人被解雇。
articles.title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
articles.content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf

articles.title: The Missing Piece in John Mark Comer’s Quiet Time
articles.summary: ‘Into the Quiet’ effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture.
articles.summary_zh: 根据近期的皮尤研究研究,超过半数的美国成年人报告说在智能手机上花费了太多的时间. 即使是承认智能手机成瘾负面影响的人,也觉得很难削减。 过度的屏幕时间不仅会损害我们的生产力和与其他人的联系, John Mark Comer在其最新著作《静默:在噪音的世界中追随耶稣》中认为,“折磨一种孤独、静默和静静的习俗对于繁荣的精神生活是绝对不可或缺的”(26)。
articles.title_zh: 约翰·马克·科默安静时光中缺失的部分
articles.content: According to a recent Pew Research study, more than half of U.S. adults report spending too much time on their smartphones. Even those who acknowledge the negative effects of smartphone addiction find it incredibly difficult to cut back. Excessive screen time isn’t just harming our productivity and connection with other people; it also makes practicing spiritual disciplines more challenging. In his latest book, Into the Quiet: Following Jesus in a World of Noise , John Mark Comer argues that “nurturing a practice of solitude, silence, and stillness is utterly indispensable to a flourishing spiritual life” (26). This timely book addresses important issues in a lively, engaging, and accessible manner. And though the staccato prose style sometimes borders on gimmicky, it’s never dull. Comer dons three hats, appearing as technoskeptic, therapist, and mystic. I responded differently to each: cheering the first, querying the second, and rejecting the third. Into the Quiet effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also makes questionable claims about the spiritual value of silence and promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture. Comer as Technoskeptic Comer’s consistent message is that readers need to intentionally disconnect from an increasingly noisy world. By “noise,” he means both literal sounds and the ever-present flood of distraction enabled by digital devices. The result is that “it is now possible to go through our entire lives and never be alone ” (18, emphasis original). Channeling secular authors like Jonathan Haidt and Johann Hari, Comer argues that constant noise threatens our well-being, whether we’re religious or not. But this dynamic is especially harmful for Christians. “Are we really surprised that . . . when we sit down to pray, we can barely even pay attention?” he asks (20). Our always-on lives differ greatly from the example of Jesus, who models a strategy of “retreat and return” (30). He ministers to the crowds and then withdraws to solitary places to pray (e.g., Matt. 14:23). This is the book’s strongest material, a timely warning with which I wholeheartedly agree. Comer as Therapist But then Comer moves in another direction. He advances therapeutic claims that may be helpful to some people but that aren’t clearly grounded in Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose: All of this stuff is in you . . . leaking out like toxic pollution into the water supply of your relational world . . . it’s asking to be dealt with. To be given a moment to speak, say its piece. To be healed. Released. (85) While the imprecatory psalms and the psalms of lament certainly model honest prayer before the Lord, and self-examination is clearly a biblical imperative, Comer’s specific claims seem more informed by extrabiblical therapeutic practices than by Scripture itself. Is it actually true that “naming our feelings out loud allows our bodies to process and discharge pain without it getting lodged in our cores” (100)? That doesn’t sound like Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose. The primary biblical support he gives for the practice of naming feelings to discharge pain is Jesus’s prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, an incident that provides the “template” for “the moments of our own Golgothas” (101). The problem is that Jesus in the garden isn’t surfacing old “toxic pollution” from “the water supply of [his] relational world” with an eye toward therapeutic healing (85). He’s facing an imminent crisis and asking the Father for either deliverance from or strength to face the trial set before him. Whatever the value of surfacing past trauma, Gethsemane doesn’t establish Comer’s claims on that point. Comer as Mystic It will be unsurprising for those who have followed Comer’s work, but he also emphasizes a form of mysticism that seeks direct, unmediated contact with God. This mysticism is an “aspect of our inner life” that is “a line of poetry from God . . . words fail here.” He concludes, “All I know is, when we sink down below the surface of all our busy, noisy, anxious minds, there is a vast ocean of peace deep inside . . . Oneing God” (194). For Comer, this intense spiritual experience can be equated with the Reformed doctrine of union with Christ. He argues, “Reformed Protestants use totally different language for a remarkably similar idea; they laud the joy of ‘union with Christ’” (192). Though it has experiential aspects and is sometimes referred to as “mystical union,” in Reformed theology “union with Christ” refers, in the first instance, to the objective work of the Holy Spirit through which a person is joined to Christ through faith and receives all his benefits thereby. It’s not a Reformed shorthand for a heightened, subjective, mystical experience that comes and goes. Though Comer identifies as a Protestant, he relies on numerous quotations from “desert fathers and mothers,” medieval mystics, and modern Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox theologians to justify his cafeteria approach to spirituality . As in his previous work, he engages with few heirs of the Reformation. Comer insists that Scripture is essential, but, for him, it doesn’t stand alone. Consistent with this non-Protestant mystical tradition, the book strongly emphasizes subjective, immediate communication from God apart from God’s inspired words in Scripture. He writes, “While Scripture is arguably the most important, and certainly the most authoritative way, we hear God’s voice, it’s not the only one” (180). In addition to the Bible, Comer stresses that we should “listen to the thoughts that come into our minds from God himself” (182). These messages arrive as the “faint whisper in the silence of our hearts,” and Comer claims that “hearing God’s voice” in this way is “just like learning to recognize any other voice” (183). Comer insists that Scripture is essential, but, for him, it doesn’t stand alone. Beyond asking whether a theological claim explicitly contradicts Scripture, we should also ask whether the Bible positively teaches it. Here’s where Comer’s presentation breaks down. Though Comer highlights mystical theologians who support his perspective, little biblical evidence supports the notion that one should, as a regular, ordinary part of the Christian life, expect God to speak apart from Scripture. Comer cites Elijah hearing the “still small voice” of God (1 Kings 19:12, KJV) and Jesus’s statement that “[his] sheep hear [his] voice” (John 10:27). Yet he provides no biblical argument for why God’s miraculous dealings with an Old Testament prophet should be taken as normative today, nor does he explain how the context of John 10 supports the idea that Jesus is referring there to the sort of “hearing” that Comer has in mind. Sola Scriptura or Silence? Untethering communication with God from Scripture often allows people to move in unhelpful and potentially spiritually dangerous directions. According to Comer, in addition to knowing God through his word, “there are aspects of God that you can experience only in the quiet” (173). If Comer simply means that we must shut out noisy distraction to truly focus on biblical truth then there would be no problem. But he seems to be saying something more. While it is not always entirely clear what Comer believes will happen in the quiet, he seems to teach that direct divine encounter through silence provides a second and separate path to knowing God. “We enter the quiet to search for God himself. To encounter him , to hear his voice, and to know his love” (172). 根据近期的皮尤研究研究,超过半数的美国成年人报告说在智能手机上花费了太多的时间. 即使是承认智能手机成瘾负面影响的人,也觉得很难削减。 过度的屏幕时间不仅会损害我们的生产力和与其他人的联系,
John Mark Comer在其最新著作《静默:在噪音的世界中追随耶稣》中认为,“折磨一种孤独、静默和静静的习俗对于繁荣的精神生活是绝对不可或缺的”(26)。 这本及时的书以生动活泼、参与和无障碍的方式处理了重要问题。 虽然这种散文风格有时会与 gi相接,
来者会戴三顶帽子 以技术怀疑者、治疗师和神秘主义者的身份出现 我对每一个都作出了不同的反应:欢呼第一个,询问第二个,拒绝第三个.
静悄悄地有效地批评了我们严酷的文化时刻的弊端,但也对静悄悄的精神价值提出了令人怀疑的主张,并提倡一种精神性,这种精神性可能会很快脱离圣经. 读者需要有意与日益吵闹的世界断绝联系。
他所说的“噪音”既指文字上的声响,又指数字设备所促成的无时无刻不在的分散注意力。 其结果是,“现在有可能经历我们的整个生活,从不孤独......”(18,强调原文)。 comer指出, 不断的噪音威胁着我们的福祉, 无论我们是否信奉宗教。
但这种动态对基督徒特别有害. “当我们坐下来祷告时,我们甚至几乎不能注意,我们真的感到惊讶吗?” 我们始终不渝的生活与耶稣的榜样大不相同,耶稣树立了“遣返和返回”战略(30)。 他向人群派遣大臣,然后撤往单独地点祈祷(如马特14:23).
这是这本书最强的材料, 来者作为治疗师, 但随后,来者向另一个方向移动。 他提出治疗性要求,

(85) 虽然圣诗和哀叹的圣诗无疑是上帝面前的模范诚实祷告,而且自我检查显然是圣经的必经之义,但比起《圣经》本身,科默尔的具体说法似乎更能从圣经外的治疗做法中得到启发。
事实上,“大声点出我们的感受,使我们的身体能够处理和释放痛苦,而不将痛苦放在我们的核心中”(100),这是真的吗? 这听起来不像圣经。 据Comer说,孤独迫使一种与痛苦的对峙,这为基本的心理目的服务.
耶稣在Gethsemane的花园里祈祷,这是他为“我们自己的Golgothas(101)时刻”提供“时代”的主要圣经支持。 问题在于花园里的耶稣并没有从“关系世界的供水”中冒出老“有毒污染”,
他正面临迫在眉睫的危机, Gethsemane并没有证明Comer对此的主张。

文字在这里失败。” 他最后说,“我所知道的是,当我们沉没在一切忙碌、吵闹、焦急的头脑之下时,内心深处是一片巨大的和平之海......团结的上帝”(194年)。 对于科梅尔来说,这种强烈的精神体验可以等同于改革后的与基督结合的学说. 他争辩说,“改革后的新教徒对一个非常相似的想法使用完全不同的语言;
他们赞扬 " 与基督联合 " 的喜悦(192年)。 虽然它具有经验性,有时被称为“神秘结合”,但在改革神学“与基督的结合”中,它首先指的是圣灵的客观工作,通过这种工作,一个人通过信仰与基督结合,从而获得他的所有利益。
这并非一个经过改革的简写, 尽管科默尔将自己确定为新教徒,但他依靠许多来自“沙漠的父亲和母亲”中世纪神秘主义者和现代罗马天主教和东方东正教神学家的引文来证明他对精神的食堂方法是正确的。
和之前的作品一样,他与改革派的少数继承人交往. 但对于他来说, 这本书与这种非预言的神秘传统一致,除了圣经中上帝启迪的话外,大力强调主观的,与上帝的即时沟通.
他写道,"虽然圣经可以说是最重要的,当然也是最权威的方法,但我们听到的是上帝的声音,但这不是唯一的声音"(180). 除了圣经之外,Comer强调,我们应该“倾听从上帝那里传入我们脑海里的思想”(182年)。
这些讯息是“在我们的心声中低语”,而Comer声称,以这种方式“听到上帝的声音”“就像学会识别任何其他声音”(183)。 但对于他来说,
除了询问神学主张是否明确与"圣经"相矛盾外,我们还应询问"圣经"是否正面教导它. 以下为Comer的演讲内容。
虽然Comer强调支持他观点的神秘神学家,但鲜有圣经证据支持这样的观念,即作为一个基督教生活中的常态,普通部分,人们应该期待上帝能与圣经分开说话. Comer引述了Elliah听到上帝的 " 仍然很小的声音 " (国王19:12,KJV)和耶稣的说法: " 他的羊听到他的声音 " (John 10:27)。
然而,他并没有提出圣经上的论点,说明为什么今天上帝与一位旧约先知的神奇交易应该被视为规范,他也没有解释约翰十世的背景如何支持耶稣在那里指的就是来宾所想的那种“倾听”的想法。 索拉脚本还是沉默?
与上帝的沟通从圣经中脱节,往往可以让人们在无益和潜在的精神危险的方向上移动. 据Comer说,除了通过他的话来认识上帝之外,“上帝有些方面你只能在静静中体验到”(173).
如果Comer只是意味着我们必须 避免吵闹的分心 真正专注于圣经的真理 那么就没有问题了 但他似乎在说更多话 虽然并非总能完全清楚科默尔认为在静默中会发生什么,但他似乎教导说,通过沉默直接的神性相遇为了解上帝提供了第二条和单独的路径.
“我们进入静悄悄地寻找上帝。 与他相遇,听到他的声音,并了解他的爱"(172). 我理解他的意思是,这个神圣的相遇和声音与我们单独从《圣经》中得到的东西是不同的。 在这方面,他引用了Avila(1515-1582年)的反改革神秘特蕾莎的话说:“`将自己安置在孤独之中'。

articles.title: What Does It Mean to Be Human?: 12 Theses Answer a Pressing Question
articles.summary: Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good.
articles.summary_zh: 今天的问题莫过于: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断加深,关于人性的辩论再次出现。 文化现在似乎持有两种相互矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质的生物, 或者我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 对上帝的拒绝导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆并不奇怪。
articles.title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
articles.content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. Similarly, those who are cognitively impaired still have the potency or essential capacity of reason and volition even though it manifests differently than in others, and even if the exercise of those powers is only actualized in the resurrection. (By contrast, a hypothetically resurrected squirrel will never actualize powers of rationality, because it was never in its nature to possess this capacity.) If humans are the particular creatures called to be in communion with and representatives of God, then such potencies are precisely those presupposed to make them fitting for the task. This focus on what human beings are , with its attendant formal capacities (or essential potencies), then, doesn’t introduce a gradation for the image of God but rather complements and grounds the emphasis on human dignity. Every human is made in the image of God, whether or not he or she actualizes wisdom or righteousness. 3. Just as the visible creation witnesses to the invisible God, the image of God includes the body, as shown in its created goodness, dependence, and fittingness for the soul. The body is a fitting home for the soul, and the soul is, in turn, the form of the body. As embodied souls, humans image God through their sexed bodies, and their personalities are communicated by way of embodiment. God has created our bodies good , has assumed one in the incarnation, and is committed to resurrect them in the consummation of the new creation. The body is thus a reminder of humanity’s humility and exaltation (Ps. 8). Humans represent God and yet absolutely depend on God. Humans are privileged to be embodied. Grasping our distinctiveness—even from that of the angels—can help us think well about artificial intelligence. Consider the parallels between angels and AI: Both are free from bodily limitations, both are said to be more intelligent than humans (although, angels also have a unique intelligence that AI cannot possess), both have longer lifespans, and both have access to a wealth of information that no human does. One might ask the question this way: If the angels were created a little higher than humanity (v. 5), why is it good for us , not them, to be the image and representation of God? The answer lies in our embodied agency and relational responsibilities toward one another. Wisdom and righteousness are embodied virtues. We bear unique responsibility for the other, as we share familial and natural relations with each other. Angels and AI cannot replicate this familial or physical bond and thus cannot participate in the care and love intrinsic to human relations and requisite for human wisdom and righteous love for God and neighbor. When a human is righteous or fails to be righteous, his community rises or falls with him. AI can neither take the blame nor be responsible for the well-being or demise of humanity; it cannot come alongside humanity and participate in its embodied experiences, suffering, or joy. The responsibility for AI is traceable back to its producers and users. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI, but it enriches human existence with a complex web of relations and a redemptive-history into which angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12) and about which silicon machines cannot know. 4. The image of God entails stewarding and cultivating creation: the cultural mandate. The cultural mandate is the vocational aspect of the image of God. God calls human beings to be fruitful and multiply (Gen. 1:28), and this involves not merely procreation but also the cultivation of creation through the formation of culture. If God creates out of nothing, humans create out of nature. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI. As human beings spread across the globe, so is the glory of God spreading through human representation. This natural development leads to the affirmation that cultural diversity itself is good. Given the fall, however, cultural diversity is mired in sin and leads to much conflict and division. This side of the fall, the cultural mandate is carried out not merely by the natur
articles.content_zh:
今天的问题莫过于: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断加深,关于人性的辩论再次出现。 文化现在似乎持有两种相互矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质的生物,
或者我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 对上帝的拒绝导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆并不奇怪。 圣经教义认为我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,但作为创造之冠却具有尊严。
随着人工智能的出现和关于种族、性别和性问题的持续辩论的到来,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学并不仅仅是学术练习. 它触及我们是谁的心脏, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。
一个基督教神学人类学 得到我们的核心 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。
在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和经改革的天主教神学人类学,我在全书中对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中落脚。 1. 所有的人都是以三月神的形象塑造的,因此被召唤来代表、享受和永远颂扬上帝。
上帝根据他的形象创造每个人。 创世纪1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个三角神是人类的原型,对于三位一体的每个人来说,都有一个独有的神性物质(另见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而创造的,因此是宗教的生物,被赋予与他们的起源有共性.
因此,每个人都是善良、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教,
我们拒绝承认真主是我们的末日,我们寻求享受,我们崇拜善神,创造现实,使它达到极点。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。
上帝以智慧和意志能力创造人性,他号召人通过正确行使正义、圣洁和真正知识的才能来代表他。 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有两个元概念很重要:行为和效力。
强力(potency)是指区分某种特定事物与其他种类的自然力量,行为是指行使这种力量. 例如,人类是具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。
Edward Feser澄清说,在主张存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应。  . 因此,我的写作能力必须与这种或那种实际的、特别的写作行动区分开来,作为后者的长期先决条件。
因此,婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的人继续是形象的持有者,即使智慧或意志的力量根本没有实现。
同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,即使这种能力的表现与他人不同,即使这些权力的行使只在复活时才得以实现。
(相比之下,假想复活的松鼠永远不会实现理性的力量,因为拥有这种能力在性质上从来都不是. ) 如果说人类是被召唤与上帝同在的特有生物和上帝的代表,那么这种力量正是预先假定的,使之适合任务.
关注人类的本性, 及其相应的正式能力(或基本力量), 每个人类都是以上帝的形象塑造的,无论他是否实现智慧或正义. 3个
与可见的造物见证无形的上帝一样,上帝的形象包括身体,这表现在它创造的善良,依赖,和对灵魂的适应性上. 身体是灵魂的合适家园,而灵魂又反过来是身体的形态. 作为被象征的灵魂,人类通过性别化的身体来形象上帝,他们的个性通过化身来传播.
上帝创造了我们的身体,创造了一个化身,并致力于在新创造的融合中将它们复活。 因此,该机构提醒人们注意人类的谦卑和赞美(临8)。 人类代表着上帝 却完全依赖于上帝 人类享有被体现的特权。
我们的特异性——即使是天使的特异性——可以帮助我们很好地思考人工智能。
想想天使和AI的相似之处: 两者都不受身体限制,据说两者都比人类更聪明(虽然天使也拥有AI不能拥有的独特智能),两者的寿命都更长,并且都能够获取人类无法获取的丰富信息.
人们可能会这样问:如果创造的天使比人类还要高一点(v. 5),为什么做上帝的形象和代表对我们而不是他们有好处? 答案在于我们体现的机构以及彼此的关系责任。 智慧与正义是体现的美德.
我们对另一方负有独特的责任,因为我们彼此有着家庭和自然的关系。 天使和AI不能复制这种家庭或肉体纽带,因此不能参与人类关系所固有的、人类智慧和对上帝和邻居的正义爱所必须的关爱和爱。
当人善恶或失善时,其群生或起或落. 大赦国际既不能承担罪责,也不能为人类的福祉或灭亡负责;它不能与人类并肩而来,参与其固有的经历、苦难或欢乐。 AI的责任可以追溯到它的生产者和使用者.
人类的化身并不是我们本性的一个有害弱点, 使我们比天使或AI更低级, 4. 神的形象包括管理和培养创造:文化使命。
文化使命是上帝形象的职业方面。 上帝称人类是丰硕和倍增的(Gen. 1:28),这不仅涉及生育,也涉及通过形成文化来培育创造. 如果上帝创造出虚无,人类创造出自然.
人类的化身并不是我们本质的有害弱点, 随着人类遍布全球,上帝的荣耀也通过人类代表传播. 这种自然发展导致确认文化多样性本身是好的。 然而,由于文化的衰落,文化多样性陷入罪恶之中,导致许多冲突和分裂。
秋天的这一边,文化使命 不仅仅是由天而降

articles.title_zh: 为了维持内城教会植物，采用传教士模式
articles.content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Second, we need to believe that God’s heart is particularly inclined toward the overlooked (Ps. 72:12–14) and toward those generous toward them (Prov. 14:21). Generosity should begin with planting churches; the greatest mercy we can bring to underserved communities is a healthy church. After all, Martin Luther said , “After the preaching of the gospel, the office and charge of a true and faithful pastor is to be mindful of the poor.” Let’s be mindful of the poor with the preaching of the gospel in the context of inner-city churches. Third, we need strategic minds to see that the American church can sustain inner-city churches just as we do global missionaries. It’s a foolish church that would send a missionary to unreached people groups with the promise of three years of step-down funding. Similarly, we shouldn’t send inner-city pastors and their staff members to their neighborhood with only short-term start-up money and the expectation that they’ll somehow figure out how to sustain the ministry. Fourth, we need to train inner-city missionaries. The unique subculture calls for dedicated training. Just as a newly graduated MD needs a residency in her specialty before she can practice, so seminary graduates need specialized training in urban anthropology, missiology, ecclesiology, apologetics, and preaching before planting and pastoring. They need a well-formed biblical understanding of the relationship between mercy ministry and gospel discipleship. They need to know how to handle gangs, dealers, the undocumented, and mental health challenges. All We Need If we believe the American church can’t plant healthy, Christ-exalting churches in the inner city, this will be unique in the history of modern missions. To my knowledge, the American church has never considered a people group to be beyond our reach. We mustn’t start now. Planters need to know how to handle gangs, dealers, the undocumented, and mental health challenges. We have much to gain in doing so. Foremost is the glory of Christ, whose name is to be known and worshiped everywhere. His glory alone is worth our effort. Second is the opportunity to tell of a Savior who proclaimed good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). That good news is Jesus himself, who paid the debt of sin for all people and fulfilled the promise of Isaiah: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost” (Isa. 55:1, NIV). Third, we gain God’s blessing. His heart is inclined toward the overlooked and toward those generous toward them. If we want to be blessed, we must care for the needy. We also face a great danger in not doing so. James links good deeds with genuine faith and warns that neglect of the needy is a sign of false faith: Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,” but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead. (James 2:15–17, NIV) Dead faith isn’t saving faith. Perhaps the greater danger is neglecting our inner cities, not walking down their sidewalks. The Great Commission includes our inner cities. Yet we’ve often neglected this work, believing there’s no model that allows us to plant churches in these communities. But there is. It’s the missionary model. We have all we need: a commission from Christ, the promise of his presence, the Holy Spirit, the Word of God, a clear need, and a tested model. It’s time we put that model to work here in our inner cities.
articles.content_zh:
一位牧师在一个星期天在教堂的谈话中告诉我的朋友,“你的朋友应该停止试图在内城种植教堂。 这不会发生, 我在COVID-19袭击前拜访了这个朋友 在一个单独的教堂里 谈论了我们的部,新英格兰城市教会规划。
我们的组织是新的, 我罪恶的倾向是想, 哦,你等着瞧! 我的朋友同样是防御性的。 然而这位牧师却发现了一些事情: 它很少发生,而且确实很困难。 为什么我们国家被忽略的内城的教堂种植如此罕见? 为何城市社区得不到足够的服务,却被福音教堂所忽视?
自2009年以来, 我们部的利益攸关方一直在讨论这些问题, 这些年来,我们在全职工作上学到了很多东西, 因为我们正在培育这个城市内部种植者网络。 由于两个关键原因,这项工作很艰巨。 然而, 这很重要。 基督命令我们造就所有国家的门徒(Matt.
28:19)——这包括我国的内城. 为了在这些空间里种下教堂 我们需要像传教士一样思考 问题 除非你在内城长大, 服务有跨文化的经验。 这是教堂栽培努力的第一个原因. 鲁比 Payne问读者, 你知道如何防止衣服从洗衣房被盗吗?
你知道怎么在半天内搬家吗? 你知道如何防止你的车被收回 如果你落在支付落后? 当内城男女经常有新的燃烧器电话时,他们的离散会令人兴奋。 城内牧师需要懂得如何传教,如何管理纳尔坎.
以及心怀善意的郊区基督徒静静地离开, 基督命令我们使所有国家的门徒 -- -- 包括我们民族的内城。 福音派常常觉得它只与一种文化成婚,
战后美国人从我们的城市迁移到郊区建立家园和教堂. 1940年,15%的美国人住在郊区. 到2000年,这一数字为50%。 福音派教徒在采取行动者中所占比例过高。 并塑造福音派的价值观。
贫困街区的教会很少在财政上自我维持,这是第二个挑战。 即使牧师的教堂门徒慷慨解囊, 因此,在这些地方工作的牧师们在“边上”从事另外两项工作时,却被一个需要帮助的教友殴打。 它无法持续。
我们不相信市内牧师的答案应该是双职业或三职业生活。 解决方案 解决这两项挑战的办法是可以做到的:一个得到支持的外国传教士的模式。 自18世纪后期起,教堂开始对在不熟悉的地方从事福音工作的男女进行培训和维持,他们无法指望当地人给予财政支持.
这种培训和支助模式应适用于市内教堂的种植。 我们需要的变革有四个方面。 第一种是改变心意. 我们需要福音饱和的心 理解所有的人都因罪恶而贫穷 住在无家可归营地的人与富裕的郊区有着同样的基本条件。
因为我们内心更相似, 我们的心灵必须受到基督倡议的现实的塑造,即把天堂的财富留给我们,使我们变得穷困,使我们变得富有(第8:9节)。 第二,我们需要相信,上帝的心脏特别倾向于被忽视的人(Ps.
72:12-14)和对那些对他们慷慨的人(14:21). 慷慨应该从种植教堂开始;我们能够给服务不足的社区带来最大的怜悯是健康的教堂。
毕竟,马丁·路德说,“在传福音之后,一个真正和忠实的牧师的办公室和职责是注意穷人。” 在市内教会中, 第三,我们需要有战略头脑,看到美国教会能够像我们做全球传教士一样,维持市内教堂。
将派遣一名传教士前往未触及的民众团体, 我们不应该派市内牧师及其工作人员到他们的社区去, 第四,要培养城内传教士.
独特的亚文化需要专门的训练. 正如刚毕业的MD在执业前需要她专业的居住权,因此神学院毕业生需要在城市人类学,误学,生态学,古生物学,以及播种和牧灵前传教的专业培训.
他们需要对慈悲部和福音门徒的关系有一个完善的圣经理解. 他们需要知道如何应对帮派、毒贩、无证和心理健康挑战。 我们需要的 如果我们相信美国教会不能在内城种植健康、虔诚的教堂,
据我所知,美国教会从未认为一个民族团体是我们无法达到的。 我们不应该从现在开始。 种植园主需要知道如何应对帮派、毒贩、无证者以及心理健康挑战。 这样做对我们有好处。 其前是基督的荣耀,基督的名号在各地皆为人所知和崇拜. 他的光荣值得我们努力。
第二是向穷人宣示好消息的救世主的机会(Luke 4:18). 这个好消息是耶稣自己,他为世人偿还罪恶,并且履行以赛亚的诺言:"你们都来吧,你们渴了就来水边吧,你们没有钱,就来买东西吃吧! 来,买酒和牛奶,不花钱也不花钱”(Isa. 55:1, NIV.
第三,我们得到了上帝的祝福。 他的心倾向于被忽略的人和对他们慷慨的人。 如果我们想要得到祝福,我们必须照顾需要帮助的人。 不这样做,我们也面临极大的危险。 詹姆斯将善行与真诚的信念联系起来,并警告说,忽视穷人是虚假信仰的标志:假设兄弟或姐妹没有衣服和日常食物.
如果你们中的一个人对他们说:“和平地去;保持温暖和丰厚的粮食”,但他们的身体需要却一无所获,这有什么好处? 同样地,信仰本身,如果不伴之以行动,就已经死亡. 死亡的信仰并不能拯救信仰。 也许更大的危险是忽略了我们的内城,而不是走在他们的人行道上。 大委员会包括我们的内城.
然而我们常常忽视这项工作, 但确实有 这是传教士模式。 我们有我们所需要的一切:来自基督的委托,他出现的承诺,圣灵,上帝之言,一个明确的需要,以及一个经过考验的模型. 我们该把这个模型放在我们的城市里。

articles.title: Report Cards on Your Actions Won’t Fix Your Heart
articles.summary: From GLP-1s to political reposts to mindfulness streaks, we’re all keeping score. Jesus says you can’t know who you are until you look at your heart.
articles.summary_zh: 我是谁? 所有文化,人类哲学,宗教制度都试图以导致有意义的生活的方式来回答这个问题. 我们想在他们中间找到一条道路,使我们能够说:“我是谁? 我是个好人。
articles.title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
articles.content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (Matt. 15:18)—who we are is revealed only when we ask questions that get at the primary motives and desires within our hearts. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. It’s not enough to obey the sixth commandment, “Do not murder,” by simply performing your nonviolent lifestyle to others for their approval. Jesus says we can’t say what kind of person we are until we’ve asked if anger, aggression, or violence reside within our heart (Matt. 5:21–22). Similarly, the Pharisees said that we are to love our neighbor but hate our enemy (Matt. 5:43). But Jesus presses deeper when he tells the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), positing that we aren’t people who love our neighbor unless we’re willing to cross cultural and racial boundaries, to be radically generous, to put ourselves and our resources at risk for the sake of others. And we won’t do those things unless we look beneath our performance and interrogate our hearts. Report-Card Life This heart-based approach remains relevant and helpful to us living within today’s culture. The Pharisaic system and Greco-Roman religion are no longer popularly practiced. But the thought that we can positively answer the question “Who am I?” through external practices and obedience to observable practices remains the norm. Though the standards and the gods look different, people are still looking to “follow the rules” toward becoming a person who lives a good life. It’s just that now there are more options and more bespoke standards. This isn’t to say our modern efforts are insignificant. Many of the examples I listed earlier can bring mental, social, and physical improvements—in some cases better than anything our world has offered before. But the problem remains the same as in Jesus’s day: These efforts ultimately don’t go deep enough. The Christian approach is that being able to know you’re a good person won’t happen by doing more and better things. To answer the question “Who am I?” in a way where I truly know that I’m living a good and right life always begins by asking, “What’s the state of my heart?” Modern trends and philosophies tend to frame life around practices, rituals, procedures, or routines. It’s a report-card framework: How many times have I prayed or meditated this week? How much money have I donated this year? How many times have I worked out this week? From Report Card to Relationship Christianity presents a different framework, one that gets at the heart. Christianity helps us see our hearts through a relational lens: “Whom or what do you worship? Whom or what do you love?” It then leads us to the answer we need for those questions: “We need a heart that will worship and love what’s good and right.” This is why the gospel stands out as the most complete story and the most effective way to answer the question “Who am I?” The doctrine of sin examines our heart and diagnoses the real problem. It shows us how God is the source of all that’s good and right and how human beings, in having sinned against God, are now far away from him. This means that even our best efforts toward being good come up short. The gospel stands out as the most complete story and the most effective way to answer the question, ‘Who am I?’ The doctrine of Christ’s sacrificial death and atonement for sins then shows the way to fix the problem. Christ, in giving up his life and atoning for our sin, bridged the gap between us and God, a bridge we can cross by faith and trust in Christ. Finally, the doctrine of redemption and regeneration by the Holy Spirit shows us that our reconnection to God through Jesus also is about transformation. We get new hearts, ones no longer compromised or enslaved by our sinful motives and desires. These new hearts help us live into what’s good and right, because we now have hearts that truly do worship and love God. As Titus 3:5–6 says, we’re saved “not because of works done by us in righteous
articles.content_zh:
我是谁? 所有文化,人类哲学,宗教制度都试图以导致有意义的生活的方式来回答这个问题. 我们想在他们中间找到一条道路,使我们能够说:“我是谁? 我是个好人。 我是一个过着良好和正确生活的人。 今天,为善良和正义提供了哪些途径? 他们与往常一样,
一个流行的途径是通过医疗改进来优化你的生活,从整形手术到GLP-1不等. 你越能"人类马克思"你的身体看起来越健康,越强壮,你就越有可能被认为是理想的人——一个能雇佣、成为朋友、约会或结婚的好人。 政治参与是另一条共同道路。
你的善良取决于你和特定政治运动的关系 当你迅速确保自己喜欢并重播所有Zohran Mamdani的影片时, 或侮辱喜欢Mamdani的人。 我们的文化为美好生活提供的道路常常是结合在一起的。
你对一个人有多好的感觉,是通过你从事治疗的时间、你在学校志愿工作多少小时、你的记忆应用有多长来衡量的。
Tara Isabella Burton在她的著作《陌生的Rites:新宗教为一个无神的世界》中认为,人们通过借鉴各种宗教和哲学,形成了自己的宗教体系。
人们已经成为“他们自己所讲的宗教的创造者,混合和配合精神和美学以及体验和哲学传统。” 我们正在做一个DIY项目, 抓住和整理我们周围的一切, 希望我们能想出一些东西来帮助我们的旅程。 那么,基督教为我们保证我们过着美好和正义的生活提供了什么途径?
记分 基督教的方法是解决圣经所说的心脏. 心灵是圣经中描述你推动和激励你的部分的短篇小说, 基督教从心脏开始,因为这是你能够确定你是谁和需要改变的唯一真正方法.
在耶稣与法利赛人的互动中, 法利赛人面对耶稣, 餐前洗手是法利赛人制定,练习的众多宗教规则之一,并号召其他人练习.
对法利赛人来说,“我是谁?” 问题的最好答案是他们遵守既定标准的情况。
如果一个人能遵守标准并过上可以遵守所有规则的生活,那么此人可以肯定地对自己和周围的人说,“我是个好人,正在过着良好和正确的生活。” 耶稣在卢克18:9–14关于法利赛人的故事是另一个例子.
法利赛人在祷告中故意记下他如何与旁边的收税者不同的是,每周斋戒两次,并总是给满十分之一. 耶稣将马太福音6中的法利赛人描述为确保他们的定期祷告能被所有人看到和肯定的人. 法利赛人并不孤单。 格雷科-罗马宗教有自己的规则和标准可以遵循。
其神灵要求祭祀,祭祀,以及节日来安抚和尊崇他们. 这样就能保证他们的生活是善良和正义的。 但耶稣重新定义了法利赛人的质疑,
正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 而谓观心. 耶稣说, " 口中流出的东西来自心脏 " (Matt. 15:18)——只有当我们提出我们心中主要动机和愿望的问题时,我们才被揭示出来。
正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 仅仅向他人表达非暴力的生活方式, 在问到愤怒、攻击或暴力是否存在于我们心中之前,
5: 21–22 (英语). 同样,法利赛人说,我们要爱我们的邻居,但恨我们的敌人(马特5:43)。
但耶稣在向好撒玛利亚人(Luke 10:25-37)的比喻说出我们不是热爱邻居的人时, 我们不会做这些事情, 除非我们看在我们的表演的底部,
报告卡生命 这种以心为本的做法对我们生活在今天的文化中仍然有意义和有帮助。 法里赛克制度和格里科-罗马宗教不再被普遍信奉. 但是,关于我们能够通过外部做法和服从可观察到的做法而积极回答“我是谁?” 问题的想法仍然是常态。
尽管标准与神看起来不同,人们仍然期待“遵守规则”,成为过上美好生活的人。 现在有更多选择, 我们的现代努力并非微不足道。
我前面列举的许多例子可以带来精神、社会和身体方面的改善——在某些情况下,这些改善比我们世界以前提供的任何改善都好。 但问题与耶稣时代一样: 这些努力最终不够深入。 基督教的观点是, 能够知道你是一个好人,
在回答“我是谁?”问题时,我真正知道,我正在过着美好和正确的生活,但首先要问:“我的心状况如何?” 现代趋势和哲学往往围绕着惯例,仪式,程序,或常规来设定生命. 这是一个报告卡框架: 这周我祈祷或冥想了多少次? 我今年捐了多少钱?
这星期我练了多少次? 从"报告卡"到"关系基督教"提供了一个不同的框架,一个得到心脏的框架. 基督教帮助我们通过一种关系视角来看待我们的心:“你们崇拜谁或什么?
你爱谁或什么?” 然后,它引导我们找到我们需要的这些问题的答案 : “ 我们需要一颗将崇拜和热爱善与正确之心。 ” 因此,福音是回答“我是谁? 罪的学说审视了我们的心脏,诊断出了真正的问题.
它向我们展示了上帝是如何成为一切善和正确之源的,以及人类如何在对上帝的罪过面前远离他。 这意味着,即使我们为成为好人所做的最大努力都不够。
福音是回答这个问题的最完整和最有效的方法,“我是谁?” 基督的牺牲和对罪的赎罪的学说,然后表明了解决问题的方法。 基督,通过放弃他的生命和赎罪,弥合了我们和上帝之间的鸿沟,我们可以通过信仰和对基督的信任而跨越一座桥梁.
最后,圣灵的救赎和再生学说向我们表明,我们通过耶稣与上帝的再联系也是关于转变的. 我们得到新的心脏,那些不再被我们的罪恶动机和欲望所牺牲或奴役。 这些新心能帮助我们活到善与善,
正如Titus 3:5-6所说,我们之所以被拯救,不是因为我们在正义中所做的工作。

articles.title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
articles.content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. articles.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
articles.summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
articles.summary_zh: Rocky在50年前的电影院首映, 1976年, 紧接着是一部布洛克和批判性的亲爱的电影(1976年最令人毛骨悚然的电影和最佳影片奥斯卡奖得主),从此成为美国电影院的一部泛神电影. 洛基在费城的布局和劣势中,对富人的故事抓住了美国令人费解的乐观情绪,这在1970年代中期给了人们必要的灵感,今天仍然有共鸣。 现在在2026年——美国半百周年—— 洛基正在获得戏剧再释放 而一部新电影,I Play Rocky(今天在部分剧场出演)讲述了标志性电影的发展故事,这部电影是它本身的逊色史诗.
articles.title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
articles.content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. He valets at a swanky Hollywood restaurant to pay the bills while he churns out scripts that he tries to get into influential hands. Sasha types the scripts for him and encourages him at every turn, even as they struggle to pay rent. At one point, she reminds him, “It’s not just you against the world. It’s us against the world.” She’s his ally and cheerleader, believing in him when few else do. Stallone’s parents were divorced, and he had a complicated relationship with his father, Frank (Matt Dillon). Yet I Play Rocky doesn’t play the “blame my parents for all my trauma” card—which is also refreshing. At one point, Stallone says, “My dad, he messed up a lot. But it’s my life.” Stallone doesn’t blame anyone else for the bad choices he’s made or the setbacks he’s had. His story is his own. At a time when it seems every other movie is some version of therapeutic moral absolution for sinners and villains , on account of their broken upbringing, it’s nice to have a movie that pushes back against this. “It’s my story,” Stallone tells the producers who want to turn his Rocky script into a film. “So I play Rocky.” Searching for Stories We used to just tell stories. Now we tell stories about stories. We write books about story and the spiritual deprivation of a destoried world . We hunger for old stories but struggle to invent new ones . Hence the appeal of a movie like I Play Rocky , which finds new narrative inspiration only by mining a classic. Our contemporary world is so uprooted, so unplaced in space and time, so rattled and wearied by what Hartmut Rosa calls “ social acceleration ,” that we feel removed or alienated from our own stories. We’re simultaneously hyperskeptical of the stories we’re told (you see this clearly in the popularity of You Can See Everything ) and deeply hungry to find our own story, to be situated in a compelling narrative that’s going somewhere and has redemption, purpose, a point. This is metamodernism’s complicated relationship with story. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling—at least in the subjective, “my story” sense. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling. Perhaps it’s downstream from social media turning us all into performers for audiences, but it feels like there’s a pressure to “find your story” (a.k.a. your brand/niche), own it, and guard it from others who might want to manipulate or leverage it for their purposes. The 2026 comedy Power Ballad touches on some of these themes of creative ownership, as does Taylor Swift in her “Taylor’s Version” series of rerecorded albums. The recent movie Digger explores the way creative control and story-crafting can be PR—shaping one’s image or the reputation of someone you love. I Play Rocky is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told. As much as this sort of storytelling is pitched as empowerment and agency, however, it also feels burdensome and exhausting. Do we really find freedom when we’re constantly obsessing over our story, or our backstory (e.g. TikTok “lore drop” trend ), and how it’s perceived by online fans and followers? The story poverty in today’s world won’t find a satisfying resolution in hyperindividuated narrative obsession. What we really need is a grander story—something bigger than “my story,” bigger than your story. What’s truly freeing is not owning our own story but seeing ourselves as part of God’s story—owned by him, our lives not our own. This is our only hope in life and death .

articles.summary_zh: 最近,我(和我的同龄人)经历了一些皈依天主教的教区人士. 我和这些皈依者交谈时, 他们发现在将面包和葡萄酒与耶稣的身体和血进行鉴别方面受到鼓励。 我听到过这样的话:乔治牧师,我喜欢耶稣在谈论主的晚餐,他说,“谁吃我的肉,谁喝我的血,谁在我体内,我就在他体内”(John 6:56)。 如果我每天把耶稣带到我的身体里, 虽然这种现象似乎更频繁地发生,
articles.title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
articles.content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. As a result of Jesus’s incarnation and death, God the Father established what Calvin calls a “holy brotherhood” between his Son and those united to his human flesh in salvation. What assurance! 2. The supper confirms and increases faith. Calvin sees the supper as a public and dramatic statement that God has atoned for the sins of the elect. God gives us this dramatic reenactment because he loves us. He knows “our faith is slight and feeble” and “unless it be propped up on all sides and sustained by every means, it trembles, wavers, totters, and at last gives way.” The Lord’s supper is a God-ordained means of “propping up” our faith, not because the supper is necessary to confirm God’s Word but because it improves our faith. In the supper, we experience a dramatic reenactment in which the ascended Christ, through his Holy Spirit, lifts our hearts to heaven. Christ does this for us, Calvin says, because regular communion with him strengthens us for the spiritual discouragements that inevitably come through besetting sin, temptation, and trials. Calvin views the sacraments as a means that cause Christ to “grow in us” so that our faith is fed more and more with Christ himself. Christians may experience any number of trials throughout their weeks that cause Christ’s spiritual, unseen realities to feel less plausible and real. Yes, our weak faith “trembles, wavers, and totters.” But when we come to the table, Christ gives us a public, dramatic reenactment that confirms his reality to our consciences and increases our faith. 3. The supper motivates and enables obedient Christian living. Calvin says, “There cannot be a spur which can pierce us more to the quick than when He makes us, so to speak, see with the eye, touch with the hand, and distinctly perceive the inestimable blessing of feeding on His own substance.” Thus, at the table, says Calvin, we’re compelled to a new obedience rooted in a grateful response to the blessings we receive there in Christ. Calvin’s conviction that the Lord’s supper provides occasion for this grateful celebration and response led him to structure worship services with this emphasis. In Calvin’s order of worship, the whole service is one long expression of gratitude in which the worshiper brings every aspect of his sin-sickness to the Savior. It concludes at the table where believers gratefully witness the Lord’s healing of all diseases dramatized. Calvin wouldn’t allow worshipers to enjoy this gratitude in private, because it’s a gift to share and a motivation that fuels outward and practical acts of “faith and charity” to others. This aspect of the supper that drives the worshiper closer to his brothers and sisters in Christ is the final distinctive of Calvin’s sacramental theology. Living Out Our Union with Christ As Christ, from love, pours out his life for the believer, the believer also pours out his life for others. So, each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. Each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. So, the next time you come to the Lord’s table, come expectantly. The living, risen Christ will use communion as fuel for your spiritual growth.

最近,我(和我的同龄人)经历了一些皈依天主教的教区人士. 我和这些皈依者交谈时, 他们发现在将面包和葡萄酒与耶稣的身体和血进行鉴别方面受到鼓励。
我听到过这样的话:乔治牧师,我喜欢耶稣在谈论主的晚餐,他说,“谁吃我的肉,谁喝我的血,谁在我体内,我就在他体内”(John 6:56)。 如果我每天把耶稣带到我的身体里, 虽然这种现象似乎更频繁地发生,
几年前,我和一个男人一起 为我们市的另一位牧师服务 我之前没有见过这个人;我只知道他直到最近才成为一所改革派和福音派神学院的教授。 这个人在耶稣召来福音的大臣的号召上宣扬一个坚实的信息,我为此感谢他. 第二天 我看见他在电视上接受采访
正如他所解释的,我需要比我的传统 更现实的,所以在午餐时,我会走进罗马天主教的教区, 并带上优待者。 从字面上讲,与耶稣的身体和血相融合,比起我教会所教的“与基督结合的神话”,我感到更加满意。 于是,我辞去了神学院的职务,回到了罗马.
我也可以和那些脱离改革信仰,加入罗马天主教、东正教或天主教传统的人交谈。 一个类似的主题贯穿于所有这些方面:渴望一个比改革后对主的晚餐提供的看法更具有转型性、感官性的现实。 这种批评是否有效?
约翰·卡尔文(John Calvin)会如何回应批评, 如果你遵循改革后的晚餐观点, 改革后的基督教徒只谈论圣餐内容, 我痛苦地意识到我在这方面的缺点。
这可能会无意中促使一些信徒在其他传统中寻求更“真正的”经验。 我们可以在辩论面包和葡萄酒的确切性质时, 今天这顿饭应该如何改变我? 让我们回顾加尔文的圣餐教义。
我们将会重新恢复对桌子的憧憬, 简言之,加尔文告诉我们,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们应当每一次都期待地坐到桌子上。
他写道, 晚餐至少以三种方式刺激信徒的精神成长。 1. 晚餐保证了我们在基督的遗产。 加尔文教耶稣用他的桌子来保证我们的遗产. 他不只是说晚餐会给我们心理上的刺激。
他的意思是,保证是通过基督和信徒之间的真正结合而得到的,他的意思是,我们通过忠实地分享契约餐食来加快这种结合的经验。 加尔文向我们展示,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们应当期待每一次都到餐桌来。
Calvin在对以弗所发表的评论中写道:“保罗说,
难道我们不知道吗?在主的晚餐里,他把他的身体伸出来,让我们享受,使我们获得永恒的生命。 加尔文坚持认为,根据信仰,基督徒是耶稣肉体人体的成员,所以在圣餐时,我们体验与他精神结合的所有好处.
基督将肉体带到他升天的状态下,他将成为信仰者的正义之道,将基督人类生命所完成的一切注入他体内。 由于耶稣的化身和死亡,上帝之父建立了加尔文所称的"神圣的兄弟情谊",他的儿子和那些在救赎中与他的人类肉团结在一起的人之间. 什么保证! 2. 国家
晚餐证实并增加了信心. 加尔文认为晚餐是公开和戏剧性的声明,上帝为选举人的罪孽赎罪. 上帝给了我们这个戏剧性的重现 因为他爱我们。
他知道“我们的信仰微乎其微,软弱无力”和“除非它被铺设在四面并用各种手段维持,否则它会颤抖、摇摆、摇摆,并最终让位”。 主的晚餐是上帝授意的“巩固”我们信仰的手段,不是因为晚餐是证实上帝之言所必需,而是因为它提高了我们的信仰。
在晚餐中,我们经历了一场戏剧性的重现,其中升天的基督通过他的圣灵将我们的心灵升到天堂. 加尔文说,基督这样做是为了我们, 因为与他定期的圣餐会 加强了我们的精神阻力 不可避免地通过 制造罪恶、诱惑和考验。
加尔文认为圣体是使基督“成长于我们”的一种手段,使我们的信仰越来越多地与基督同在。 基督教徒在他们的几周里可能会经历许多考验,
是的,我们软弱的信仰“三联、摇摆和摇摆 ” 。 但是,当我们来到议席时,基督给了我们一个公开的,戏剧性的重现,证实了他对我们良知的现实,增加了我们的信仰. 3. 晚餐激励并促成服从基督教的生活。
加尔文说 , “ 没有比他造就我们时更能快速地刺穿我们的刺脚的了,比如说,用眼睛看,用手摸,并清楚地看到用他自己的物质来喂食的不可估量的祝福。 ” 因此,加尔文说,我们被迫接受一种新的服从,这种服从植根于对基督所赐福的感激之情。
加尔文相信主的晚餐为这一感恩的庆典和回应提供了契机,因此他以此为着重点构建了礼拜服务. 在加尔文的崇拜顺序中,整个礼拜是长期表达的感激之情,其中崇拜者将他的罪恶症的方方面面带到救世主身上.
最后,信徒们感谢地见证了上帝治愈了戏剧化的所有疾病。 加尔文不允许崇拜者私下享受这种感恩, 因为这是分享的礼物,
晚餐的这个方面让礼拜者在基督中更接近他的兄弟姐妹,是加尔文神圣神学的终极特色. 与基督同归于尽,从爱中为信徒倾注生命,信徒也为他人倾注生命.
所以,每次你用信仰来吃主的晚餐,你都与基督一起生活,他住在你体内,并通过你来创造新的你。 每次你用信仰来吃主的晚餐,你都与基督一起生活,他住在你体内并通过你生活,使你成为新人。 所以,你下次来到主的桌子上时,应该会来。
活的,升天的基督会用圣餐作为你精神成长的燃料.

articles.title_zh: 编辑精选：全新儿童图画书
articles.content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a note in the back of Doing Something New about how she moved many times in childhood: “By the time we settled in California for seventh grade, we had lived in India, Ghana, Cameroon, England, Mexico, and New York.” Changes often come with both losses and gains, and Perkins writes with sympathy and encouragement for children walking through all sorts of new experiences. The text reminds readers to live like Jesus—showing love, courage, and kindness—with the knowledge that Jesus also walked through hard experiences and that he’s with us now, wherever we go. The pictures include what appear to be a new school, new friends, new seasons, and the potential loss of or separation from a loved one. The rhyming words offer this prayer to Christ as a resource for others experiencing changes—“You trusted God and God helped you / Here I am, Lord—help me too.” Also check out these books: Jude and the Extraordinary, Spectacular, Miraculous Day: A Creative Retelling of the Feeding of the 5,000 by Jessica Dennis Bush features beautiful mosaic illustrations that look refreshingly like real art rather than AI and a message about offering Jesus what we have. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) Made like Me: A True Story from the Beginning of Everything by Jen Wilkin (with illustrations by Rommel Ruiz) tells the story of the creation of the world with vibrant, kinetic illustrations and an emphasis on how we were designed for community from the beginning of time. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) The Mansoul Chronicles, Book 2: The Schemes and Snares of Diabolus by Tyler Van Halteren (with illustrations by Uyen Nguyen and Aleksander Jasinski) is an illustrated chapter book retelling a John Bunyan story from the 1600s with surprisingly relevant themes for Christians today. ( Amazon ) The Sweetest of Lemons by Daniel Nayeri (with illustrations by Rahele Jomepour Bell) is both a true story and a fairy tale about “a lemon so perfectly sweet it cured sadness itself.” Like the best fairy stories, it carries themes of courage, perseverance, longing, and—most importantly—hope, acknowledging hardship but resting in the certainty of goodness on the horizon. ( Amazon ) Where Wonder Leads: An Adventure in God’s Wild and Wonderful World by Eryn Lynum (with illustrations by Chiara Fedele) is from the host of the Nat Theo podcast and somehow manages to touch on grief, nature activities, profound theology, and fascinating scientific facts in just over 100 illustrated pages. ( Amazon )
articles.content_zh:
秋是变之季. 在我们家里,随着叶子变黄,日子缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学。 这意味着图片书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激的事物一起, 来一些新的东西。
许多这些书是关于大变革和适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心脏. 但有些人还谈到我们周围每天发生的一些小变化,比如在童年短暂的想象中欢笑或沉睡,准备新的一天。
在所有这些经历到达地平线后, 然后像州际告示牌一样飞过, 记得“每一个好的礼物和完美的礼物都来自上面,
当你把这些全新的书交给一个年轻的读者或整理起来一起欣赏时, 让这些故事提醒你享受这一时刻的美好, 即使它正在变成新的事物, 上帝的善良是永恒的。 一、导 言
"上帝赐予睡眠"(God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard),由贝桑·韦尔比(英语:Bethan Welby (TGC Store QQ Amazon))所描绘. 当我们的家庭疲惫不堪 并计划一个大动作 四个孩子6岁和6岁以下, 我真的可以使用 这本小书 从贝茜 Childs Howard。
上帝赐予睡眠(God Gives Sleep)是一本配有可爱动物插图(sleeping ladybugs!)的韵律板书,还有两个简单的节点,即使非常年轻的听众也可以为自己重复或“阅读 ” : “ 上帝赐予睡眠”和“上帝会保存 ” 。 两者都反映了上帝的诺言,认为对养育孩子的早期至关重要,充满了甜蜜的,困困的抱抱和漫长的,无眠的夜晚.
最后一张图片显示整个家庭都睡着,包括以赛亚40:31(“那些希望耶和华恢复力量的人,NIV”)。 上帝赐予睡眠的热情、温柔、幽默和智慧, 由Kevan Chandler和Joe Sutphin(亚马逊)改编。 全面披露:我是一个巨大的维尼粉丝。
我可能读过许多次Milne的原著, 但我喜欢这个 虽然我错过了Milne在故事部分的显著叙事,
年轻独立读者的家长经常向我征求关于书本复杂到足以参与但内容和格式适合初等学校的建议。
这个版本完全适合6至9岁的人可以通过图片追踪故事的空间,但也享受到一些复杂词汇(“突然和暂时的碰撞”)的挑战和奖励背景研究的笑话(“埋伏是一种惊喜”)。 “有时也是粗鲁。 ”
Winnie-the-Pooh:The Graphic 小说是对这一经典的幼儿期庆祝活动的甜蜜和值得称赞的,在其所有富有想象力的奇迹中. 3. 乔纳森·兰德里·克鲁斯(Jonathan Landry Cruse)的《上下、内部、不能相信的王国》, 冒险从一个儿子乞求父亲告诉他一个令人兴奋的与龙和骑士的睡前故事开始.
结果是这段福音的重现,作为与国王和王子的追求,并提醒我们在王国的卑微地位. 乔·霍克斯(Joe Hox)的插画以传统和明亮著称,
故事告诉我们,好国王将“以他的力量使我们强大起来”,这是希望为王国做大事的年轻骑士的有力信息。 4个
