articles.title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
articles.summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
articles.summary_zh: 几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上的塞门(Matt. 5-7)。 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年中, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最著名的布道 用于记忆更具有变革性。 约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道,山上的塞尔蒙人“是[耶穌]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的一件事,因为这是他自己对他希望追随者成为和做的事情的描述。
articles.title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
articles.content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. I had thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. When Jesus equates murder with anger, he exposes a corruption we prefer not to acknowledge within ourselves (Matt. 5:21–26). Later in the New Testament, we see we have a Savior who forgives our anger and frees us to live to God’s glory. Having this framework embedded in my mind helps me remember the gospel when outside influences pull my attention away. The first three years of my journey into the Sermon on the Mount have helped me be more like Jesus. Yet it’s obvious to me that my journey has just begun. My life changed when those two college students challenged me to memorize the sermon. Almost every day, those words draw me closer to my Savior and encourage me to conform to him. The Sermon on the Mount has given me more joy than any product the algorithm could ever pop into my newsfeed.
articles.content_zh:
几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上的塞门(Matt. 5-7)。 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年中, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最著名的布道 用于记忆更具有变革性。
约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道,山上的塞尔蒙人“是[耶穌]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的一件事,因为这是他自己对他希望追随者成为和做的事情的描述。” 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。
在一个算法捕捉到我们感情并通过我们的渴望引诱我们上线的世界中,我们能够采用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习和记住圣经——特别是山上的塞门. 创建新算法 算法常常比我们自己更了解我们.
每次我们在亚马逊买东西或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法会记录我们的活动, 这个简介显示了我们的真正兴趣(不只是我们在社交媒体生记中列出的那些),
在毫秒内,公司利用算法了解我们的情况,发现最有效的方法,让我们购买他们的产品. 正如算法用我们喜欢的每一个帖子和我们看的每一卷片子来了解我们一样,上帝的言语以我们学习和运用的每一个命令、我们思考的每一个诗句,以及我们采纳的作为生活方式的每一个教义,在我们的体内充满活力。
通过吸收和服从耶稣在山上的塞尔门,我们可以建立一个反馈循环,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 在开始我的回忆计划之前, 我听到许多基督徒把圣经记忆说成是符合耶稣的最有力工具之一,
当我意识到算法能比上帝的话更能进入我的生活时, 通过吸收和服从耶稣在山上的塞尔门,我们可以建立一个反馈循环,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 我和许多美国人一样,每天平均有两个多小时 滚动社交媒体和网上购物, 阅读圣经的时间要少得多。
我本以为缺乏时间是记忆圣经的最大障碍。 但实际上,我的感情和优先考虑是障碍。 纪念和研究山上的塞蒙号提供了强大的重置. 我注意到我一生中有两个重大的变化。 1. 我的思想日益为耶稣对我的愿望所吸引。
之前,我很容易被网络影响者 说我应该做什么 和我的心真正想要做什么。 现在,圣经轻轻地吸引我走向基督的恩典。 例如,几个月前,有人给我写了严酷的文字. 我无法回避我所记住的:为伤害你的人祈祷(Mt.
5:44。 在这些困难的相互作用中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一个狂欢祈祷。 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以想一想我的眼中的木头是什么(Mt.7:5). 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大不相同。
我不再觉得算法能给我一个美丽的家, 一个穿得漂亮、体格完美的女人, 当我停止停留 在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上的赛蒙 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。
这些章节给了我一个强壮的镜头,我可以通过这些镜头观看上帝的所有言语。 在喝完耶稣的布道之后,我认为这是《旧约》和《新约》所依赖的。 我以为没有时间 是我记起圣经的最大障碍 但实际上,我的感情和优先考虑是障碍。
当耶稣将谋杀等同于愤怒时,他揭露了我们不愿承认的腐败(Matt. 5:21-26)。 在后来的"新约"中,我们看到我们有一个救世主,他宽恕了我们的愤怒,让我们自由,活在上帝的荣耀中. 将这个框架嵌入我的脑海, 帮助我记住,当外部影响 吸引我的注意力。
我进入山上的塞尔门旅行的前三年帮助我更像耶稣. 但对我来说, 当两个大学生要求我记住布道时,我的生活就变了。 这些话几乎每天都让我更接近我的救世主,鼓励我服从他.
山上的赛蒙给了我更多的快乐 比任何产品 算法可能涌进我的新闻。

articles.title: Contend Without Being Contentious
articles.summary: In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments.
articles.summary_zh: “我们如何在不争吵和争论的情况下,为信仰而争辩呢? ” 我(Barry)的一位教友在研究Jude的信时, Jude在宗旨声明(vv. 3–4)中表示, 然而,他认为有必要敦促他们“继续信仰”。
articles.title_zh: 在不引起争议的情况下进行竞争
articles.content: “How do we contend for the faith biblically without becoming quarrelsome and contentious?” A member of my (Barry’s) congregation posed this thoughtful yet difficult question when our church was studying the letter of Jude. In his purpose statement (vv. 3–4), Jude says he wants to write about the salvation he shares in common with his recipients. However, he finds it necessary instead to exhort them to “contend for the faith.” What does obeying this exhortation involve? Before we contend for the faith, it’s essential to clarify how to approach confrontation and why we’re seeking to confront in the first place. Knowing myself, I (Ben) can have many sinful and unhelpful reasons for confronting; my pride often tempts me to seek my glory in confrontation rather than seeking the Lord’s glory. Yet when our motivation is wrong, our manner is too. Then, contending can quickly become contentiousness. Jude gives us a better way. Why and How To Confront His letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. Jude provides four basic confrontation categories that will help us defend the truth without becoming quarrelsome. 1. Oppose deceivers (v. 4). We must be able to distinguish between those who are confused and those who are deceivers. Not everyone who errs is a malicious false teacher. Some simply need patient guidance, instruction, and compassionate discipleship. Jude’s letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. But others actively promote error, refuse to submit to biblical authority, or sow seeds of division that can lead God’s people away from Christ. Jude has deceivers in mind as his primary concern in his letter. He’s concerned not just that they’re in error but that they’re influential. For that reason, he wants the church to have the Spirit-led courage to confront the deceivers’ errors. Such contending requires wisdom. For pastors, it can involve correcting false teaching both privately and publicly. You may need to warn your church about dangerous influences or refuse to give a platform to those who persistently distort the gospel. Remember, Paul instructs elders to rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine (Titus 1:9) and to protect God’s flock from spiritual wolves (Acts 20:28–31). He also warns congregations to watch out for divisive teachers (Rom. 16:17–18). When we confront deceivers, our aim isn’t to embarrass them or to win arguments. Rather, we contend for the faith because truth matters and because Christ’s church matters. 2. Instruct doubters (v. 22). In the Christian life, we encounter many who have doubts about the faith. They know the truth, but they struggle to believe it. Instructing those who doubt may not seem like contending for the faith at first, but gently clearing up their concerns strengthens both their faith and the church’s faith. Contending well for doubters can prevent them from wandering or even from becoming deceivers. It’s an act of mercy (v. 22), and it must be done mercifully. When believers doubt or begin to waver on the truth, our responsibility isn’t to ruthlessly force truth on them. We also shouldn’t ignore their questions. Neither response is merciful. Instead, we must engage doubters’ questions with compassion, trusting that the Lord will reveal truth to them in his time. Our belief in Scripture’s sufficiency is critical here. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. Doubts are many and various, but the Bible remains constant and trustworthy. 3. Warn wanderers (v. 23). Between doubting and deceiving stands another category: wandering. Some in the church drift, or have drifted, toward dangerous doctrinal error or patterns of sin that, if left unchecked, will lead to their fall. Jude prescribes the appropriate response: “Save others by snatching them out of the fire” (v. 23). His imagery conveys urgency. Those who wander are on the verge of spiritual catastrophe, so drastic measures are necessary. Many Christians hesitate to confront because warning a fellow church member can feel uncomfortable and intrusive. But God’s Word regularly warns. It does so sternly but as an act of love. For example, Jesus instructs believers to pursue a sinning brother so he might repent and be restored (Matt. 18:15–17). Paul tells the Galatians to restore those caught in transgression with a spirit of gentleness (6:1). And James writes that bringing back a wandering sinner saves him from destruction (5:19–20). When we confront a wanderer, the goal is never condemnation but rescue. Jude calls us to urgent action because drift is spiritually dangerous. We’re to speak the truth in love so that members of Christ’s body, from the least to the greatest, may grow in every respect to maturity under his headship (Eph. 4:15). 4. Guard your heart (vv. 20–21). In all our contending, Jude tells us to guard our hearts. This is unique among Jude’s contention categories because it’s the only one with an inward focus. When we contend, we’re on the offense, fighting for others’ souls. But we must also play defense, guarding the ground God has already claimed in our own hearts. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. How do we guard our hearts? How do we keep ourselves in the love of God (v. 21)? Jude offers three ways: build up your faith, pray, and wait expectantly for the Lord Jesus’s mercy (vv. 20–21). The first two seem obvious. Of course building your faith through God’s Word and prayer will keep you from being deceived. However, Jude’s third instruction requires more thought. Waiting seems passive, but it’s an expectant act of faith that involves grounding our hearts in the gospel—actively remembering that Jesus is the One who is able to keep us from stumbling and who will finally make us stand in his glorious presence (vv. 24–25). Before You Contend We guard our hearts because running into confrontation too hastily only results in contentiousness. This quality is unbefitting of Christians, and particularly of church leaders (1 Tim. 3:3; 2 Tim. 2:22–26). So be adequately prepared before you step in. Clarify your approach so you bring the right motivation and tone to each situation. Guard your heart, and above all, pray for yourself, your church, and those with whom you’re contending. In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments. We need elders, pastors, teachers, and faithful church members who know how to contend wisely, courageously, and graciously.
articles.content_zh:
“我们如何在不争吵和争论的情况下,为信仰而争辩呢?” 我(Barry)的一位教友在研究Jude的信时, Jude在宗旨声明(vv. 3–4)中表示,
然而,他认为有必要敦促他们“继续信仰”。 遵守这一劝告涉及什么? 在争取信仰之前,必须澄清如何对抗, 我知道,我(本)有许多罪恶和无益的理由可以对抗;
我的骄傲常常诱惑我在对抗中追求我的荣耀,而不是寻求主的荣耀. 然而,当我们的动机是错误的,我们的方式也是。 然后,争吵会很快成为争议。 裘德给了我们更好的方法。 为什么和如何对抗 他的信为基督徒提供了一个框架,以便他们辨别我们何时应该面对错误,以及面对何种程度的激烈程度。
裘德提供了四个基本的对抗类别,帮助我们捍卫真理而不成为争吵. 1. 反对欺骗者(v.4). 我们必须能够区分那些困惑和欺骗的人。 不是每个人都是恶意的假老师 有些人只需要耐心的指导、指导和同情的弟子。
Jude的书信为基督徒提供了一个框架, 但其他人却积极宣扬错误,拒绝服从圣经权威,或者播下分裂的种子,从而可以引导上帝的百姓远离基督. 朱德在信里把欺骗者当作他关心的主要问题。
他不仅担心他们出错, 因此,他希望教会有精神引导的勇气来对抗欺骗者的错误. 这种争吵需要智慧。 对牧师来说,这可能涉及纠正私下和公开的虚假教学。
你可能需要警告你的教会 危险的影响 或者拒绝给那些坚持歪曲福音的人一个平台 记住,保罗指示长者谴责那些违背声音学说的人(Titus 1:9),并保护上帝的羊群免受精神狼的伤害(Acts 20:28–31). 他也警告各会众注意分裂的教师(16:17-18).
当面对欺骗者时, 相反,我们为信仰而斗争,因为真理很重要,而基督的教会也很重要。 2. 指示怀疑者(v.22)。 在基督教生活中,我们遇到许多对信仰有疑虑的人. 他们知道真相,但他们很难相信
引导那些疑惑者一开始可能似乎并不像在争辩信仰, 善于为怀疑者服务,可以防止他们徘徊,甚至成为欺骗者。 这是慈悲的行为(v.22),
当信徒怀疑或开始动摇真相时, 我们的责任不是无情地强迫他们接受真相。 我们不应该忽视他们的问题。 这两种反应都是仁慈的。 相反,我们必须以同情心对待怀疑者的问题,相信上帝将在他那个时代向他们揭示真相。 我们相信圣经的充足性,
上帝的言语,不是我们的教义或博学技巧,拥有揭示他真相的能力。 怀疑是多方面的,但圣经始终不变,值得信赖. 3.警告流浪者(v.23). 在怀疑和欺骗之间,还有另一个类别:流浪。
一些在教堂里漂流着,或者已经漂流着,走向危险的理论错误或者罪恶模式,如果不加以控制,将导致他们的倒台。 Jude规定了适当的对策:“通过从火中抢救他人”(v.23)。 他的图像传达了紧迫性. 那些游荡的人处于精神灾难的边缘,因此必须采取严厉的措施。
许多基督徒对峙犹豫不决,因为警告一个教会成员会感到不舒服和侵扰. 但真主的命令是经常警告的。 它如此严厉,但是一种爱的行为。 例如,耶稣指示信徒追逐一个有罪的兄弟,以便他悔改并被恢复(Matt. 18:15-17)。
保罗告诉加拉提亚人要以温柔的精神(6:1)来恢复那些被抓住的违法者. 詹姆斯写道,带回一个流浪的罪人,使他免于毁灭(5:19-20). 当我们面对流浪者时,目标绝不是谴责而是拯救。 朱德要求我们采取紧急行动,因为漂移在精神上是危险的。
让基督身体的成员, 从最少到最伟大, 都能在他的领导下成长到成熟(Eph.4:15), 4. 守护心(vv. 20–21). 在我们的争吵中,裘德告诉我们 守护我们的心脏。 这在Jude的争论类别中是独一无二的,
当我们争吵的时候,我们是在犯罪,为他人的灵魂而战斗。 但我们也必须进行防守 守护上帝已经宣称的地面 上帝的言语,不是我们的教义或博学技巧,拥有揭示他真相的能力。 我们怎么保护我们的心? 我们如何让自己在上帝的爱(v.
犹大提供三种方式:建立你的信仰,祈祷,等待主耶稣的慈悲(vv. 20–21). 前二显相. 当然,通过真主的言辞和祈祷来建立你们的信心,将使你们不被欺骗。 然而,朱德的第三个指示需要更多的思考.
等待似乎是被动的, 但这是一种充满期待的信仰行为, 将我们的心灵植根于福音中, ưμ㼯A 我们保护我们的心,因为过于仓促地陷入对抗只会导致争议。
基督教徒,特别是教会领袖的这种素质是不合适的(1提姆3:3;2提姆2:22-26)。 在你介入之前要做好充分的准备 澄清你的方法 这样你就会给每个情况带来正确的动机和语气 保护你的心,最重要的是,为你自己、你的教堂和与你争吵的人祈祷。
在以神学妥协和不必要的愤慨为标志的时代,我们需要教会领袖,他们能做的不仅仅是赢得辩论. 我们需要长老、牧师、教师和忠实的教会成员,他们知道如何明智、勇敢和慷慨地进行斗争。

articles.title: Train Women to Teach the Bible: A 4-Week Plan
articles.summary: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. But where do we find teachers?
articles.summary_zh: 圣经研究是许多教会中妇女部的心跳。 越来越多的教会更喜欢现场教学, 这可能会给妇女部主任带来挑战: 我们在哪里找到老师? 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
articles.title_zh: 培训女性教导圣经： 4周计划
articles.content: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. More and more churches have come to prefer live teaching over video studies . But this can present a challenge for women’s ministry directors: Where do we find teachers? Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. Whether women have never taught the Scriptures before or are building on previous experience, we can help them grow and gain confidence in “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Tim. 2:15) through careful instruction and practice. To equip women in my church to teach, I helped develop a four-session course. Here’s how we developed and implemented this training. Get Organized I first recruited two women with experience teaching the Bible, and together we prepared ourselves as instructors by taking the online Simeon Trust First Principles for Women course. We then personalized the principles we learned to fit our training goals for other women in our church. Since there are different strategies for approaching various genres of Scripture, the first time we held this course, we chose to train women on how to teach an epistle. We selected 1 Peter as our text and assigned each group a passage to work on throughout the course. For example, Group 1 had 1 Peter 1:1–12, Group 2 had 1:13–21, and Group 3 had 4:12–19. We used 5:1–11 as a common passage that we studied as a whole group. In subsequent courses, we chose other genres of Scripture: narrative using passages from a Gospel and wisdom/poetry using a psalm. Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. We promoted the training with a clear purpose: to help participants grow in their ability to understand and teach God’s Word. We spelled out our expectations: attending all four sessions, completing homework, and teaching a 10-minute message to peers. Individual attention in training is key, so we assigned each participant to a small group of three to six women with a leader. The leader gave feedback on homework and answered questions. Teach the Course Here’s what we covered each week, including teaching content, small-group work, and homework assignments. Week 1: Foundations of Study After sharing two foundational truths about the Bible—Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16–17) and Scripture is alive and active, changing us as we study it (Heb. 4:12)—we taught three principles. First, we never add to or subtract from what’s written in the Word (Deut. 4:2; 1 Cor. 4:6; Rev. 22:18–19). A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. We must be diligent to stay faithful to the Holy Spirit’s intended meaning. We strive to “stay on the line” of Scripture , never going above it by adding to it (which can result in undue speculation or legalism) or going below it by taking away from it (avoiding unpleasant or confusing passages, or altering the meaning to what we want it to mean). Second, the Bible is one big story, with one Hero of the story (Luke 24:27). From Genesis to Revelation—creation, fall, redemption, and restoration—we see God at work to reconcile people to himself. The Old Testament points to our need for and anticipation of a Savior, and the New Testament records and reflects on that Savior. Understanding this one big story helps reveal the significance of each passage. Third, context is king and questions are key . Context is the setting in which something occurs, and it always guides our interpretation. We consider both the literary context (what comes before and after a passage) and the historical context (the situation in which the original audience found themselves). To “stay on the line,” asking in-depth questions of the passage is vital, so we introduced the participants to questions for an epistle . In small-group time, we had each woman read the group’s assigned passage aloud because a thoughtful reading aids understanding, as does hearing the passage multiple times. For homework, we asked the women to list 15 observations from their small group’s passage along with 15 observations from the common passage. Week 2: From Text to Talk We started in small groups with each woman sharing her observations on her group’s designated passage. Then we had a whole-group discussion of observations found in the common passage. This week’s teaching focused on how to go from observing a Scripture text to preparing to teach it to a group of real women. We first explained exegesis—analyzing Scripture to draw out its intended meaning. We walked the women through how to use the questions for an epistle to understand the passage’s meaning to the original recipients. We always look for the main idea, the immediate context (passages before and after in the book), the historical context (names, places, situations, other passages that may explain this one), and the biblical context (Where does this fit in the bigger story of the whole Bible?). A concordance is a valuable tool here. We then helped participants find the connection to the gospel (Luke 24:25–27). We taught them to look for related themes (e.g., hope, forgiveness, sacrifice, priesthood) and typology (people, objects, or events patterned after Jesus like Joseph, Boaz, David, or the ark). The Jesus Storybook Bible can be a great help in revealing these connections. Finally, we taught the women how to draw out applications. The main idea doesn’t change because of the audience, but the particular applications may. We emphasized knowing your audience by thinking through where the listeners are spiritually, what sin issues or struggles they have, and what encouragement they need. We reminded the group of the purpose of our messages: to have women’s affections stirred by the Spirit so they’re personally affected by the truth of the text. For homework, each woman identified an audience for her teaching specifying age, life stage, and specific needs and struggles. Then, using her assigned passage, she recorded the main idea, the significance to the original hearers, the connection to the gospel, and an application specific to her target audience. Week 3: Structure and Illustrations In small groups, women shared their homework and instructors gave feedback. While it’s time-consuming for each woman to share, everyone benefits from hearing each other’s work on the same passage. We began this week’s teaching by explaining two common mistakes teachers make: (1) sharing what “touched us” in a passage, unrelated to the main idea, and (2) having so many points that they obstruct the main idea. To avoid these mistakes, we discussed the importance of structure. The process of finding a text’s structure varies depending on its genre, so we briefly explained how to go about determining the “shape” of three genres: epistle, narrative, and poetry. Since we were learning to teach an epistle, we spent the most time on this, helping the women focus on the words and grammar. We taught them to look for “bookends” (similar words at the beginning and end of a paragraph or book); repeated words, phrases, or ideas; connecting words like if/then, because, therefore; grammar and verb tenses; and words that reveal the context. All these help uncover the author’s main idea or emphasis in a discourse. We then took time to practice identifying these elements in small groups using the common passage. A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. To close week 3, we introduced illustrations. We explained their purpose (to serve the main idea and application and make the teaching clearer) along with various illustration types and where to find them. We suggested using stories, analogies, word pictures, and examples from personal experiences, books, movies, history, current events, and nature. For homework, we asked the women to develop a teaching outline and an illustration for their passage. Week 4: Preparing a Talk The final week began in small groups with each member sharing her teaching outline and illustratio
articles.content_zh:
圣经研究是许多教会中妇女部的心跳。 越来越多的教会更喜欢现场教学, 这可能会给妇女部主任带来挑战: 我们在哪里找到老师? 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
无论妇女以前或现在都从未教授过《圣经》,我们都可以通过认真的教学和实践,帮助她们成长并树立“正确处理真理之言”的信心(2 Tim2:15)。 为了让教会里的女人能够教书,我帮助开发了四门课程。 以下是我们如何制定并实施这一培训。
Get Organization I首先招募了两位具有教授圣经经验的女性,我们一起通过在线西门信托基金妇女第一原则课程,准备成为教员。 然后,我们将我们学到的原则个性化,以适应我们为教会中其他妇女的培训目标。
由于有不同的策略 接近各种流派的圣经, 我们第一次举办这个课程, 我们选择培训妇女 如何教授一个故事。 我们挑选了一名彼得作为我们的案文,并指派每个小组在全程中工作一段。 例如,第1组拥有1 Peter 1:1–12,第2组拥有1:13–21,第3组拥有4:12–19.
我们用5:1–11作为我们作为一个整体研究的共同段落. 在随后的课程中,我们选择了其他的经典流派:使用福音书的段落进行叙事,使用诗歌的智慧/诗歌. 圣经老师不会随时来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。
我们以明确的目的促进了培训:帮助参与者提高理解和教授上帝之言的能力。 我们阐述了我们的期望:参加所有四场会议,完成作业,向同行传授十分钟的信息。 对培训的个别关注是关键所在,因此,我们指派每个参与者到一个由3至6名妇女组成的小组,并有一名领导人。
领导对功课进行反馈,回答问题. 包括教学内容、小组工作、家庭作业等。 第1周:研究基础 在分享了两个关于圣经的基本真理之后——书稿是上帝创造的(2 Tim. 3:16-17),圣经是活生生的,在我们研究圣经(Heb.
4:12)——我们教了三项原则. 首先,我们从不增减《言语》中的内容(德国4:2;1 Cor.4:6;Rev.22:18-19)。 圣经的文本不是给我们深刻见解的跳跃点。 我们必须坚持忠于圣灵的本意。
我们努力“坚持”《圣经》,从不增加(这可能导致不适当的猜测或法律主义),或从《圣经》中取下(避免令人不快或令人困惑的段落,或改变我们想要它的含义),从而超越《圣经》。 第二,圣经是一个大故事,有一个故事的英雄(公爵24:27).
从创世纪到启示——创造、堕落、赎罪和恢复——我们看见上帝在努力使人与自己和解。 《旧约》指出了我们对救世主的需求和期待,《新约》记录并反思了该救世主。 了解这个大故事有助于揭示每个段落的意义. 第三,背景是国王,问题是关键。
环境是事物发生的环境,它总是指导我们的解释。 我们既考虑文学背景(一段前后发生的事情),也考虑历史背景(原始观众发现自己的情况). 因此,我们向与会者介绍了一些问题。
我们让每位女性大声读到他们指定的段落, 关于家庭作业,我们要求妇女从其小团体的行经中列出15项意见以及共同行经中的15项意见。
第2周:从文字到谈话 我们开始分成几个小组,每个妇女都分享她对小组指定通道的看法。 然后,我们进行了关于共同段落中发现的意见的全体讨论。 本周的教学重点是如何从观察一本圣经到准备教授给一群真正的妇女。
我们首先解释了解释——分析《圣经》,以找出其意旨。 我们用这些问题来理解这些段落对原始接受者的意义。
我们总是寻找主要思想,即时背景(书中前后的通道),历史背景(名称,地点,情况,其他段落可能解释这一段),以及圣经背景(这与整个圣经中更大的故事在哪里相适应?). 在这里,协调是一个宝贵的工具。 然后,我们帮助参与者找到与福音书的联系(公爵24:25-27)。
我们教他们寻找相关的主题(如希望,宽恕,祭祀,祭祀)和类型(人,物,或以耶稣为图案的事件如约瑟夫,波阿兹,大卫,或方舟). 耶稣故事书圣经可以极大地帮助揭示这些联系. 最后,我们教妇女如何绘制申请表。
主要想法不会因为观众而改变, 我们强调通过思考听众的精神所在、他们的罪恶问题或斗争以及他们需要什么鼓励来了解听众。
我们提醒这群人我们的信息的目的:让心灵激起女性的感情, 对于家庭作业,每个妇女都指定了一个听众来指导她的教学,具体说明年龄、生活阶段以及具体的需要和斗争。
随后,她利用她指定的段落,录制了主要想法,对原听觉者的意义,与福音的连接,以及针对她目标受众的应用程序. 第3周:结构和说明 在小组中,妇女分享她们的家庭作业,教员提供反馈。
虽然每个妇女分享是耗时的,但每个人都能听到对方在同一段的作品。 我们开始本周的教学时, 解释了两个常见的错误:(1) 分享“触摸”我们的东西,
为了避免这些错误,我们讨论了结构的重要性。 寻找文本结构的过程依其流派不同而不同,所以我们简要地解释了如何决定三种流派的“形状 ” : 论语、叙事和诗歌。 自从我们学会教一个学说以来,我们花了最多的时间来研究这个问题,帮助女性专注于文字和语法.
我们教他们寻找“书尾”(一段或书开头和结尾的类似词);重复的词、短语或想法;将词语连接起来,例如如果/当时,因为这样;语法和动词紧张;以及揭示上下文的词语。 所有这些有助于在讨论中揭示作者的主要思想或重点。
然后,我们花了时间,用共同通道将这些因素分成小组。 圣经的文本不是给我们深刻见解的跳跃点。 在第三个星期结束时,我们介绍了插图。 我们解释了它们的目的(服务于主要思想和应用,使教学更加清晰)以及各种插图类型和在哪里找到它们。
我们建议使用故事,类比,文字图片,以及个人经历,书籍,电影,历史,时事和自然中的例子. 关于家庭作业,我们请这些妇女制定教学大纲和说明,供她们通过。 第4周:准备谈话 最后一周开始分成小组,每个成员分享她的教学大纲和插图

articles.title: When Morningness Is Confused with Godliness
articles.summary: Could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical?
articles.summary_zh: 你们应当在早晨和真主在一起享受。 你们应当在白昼中为真主创造最初的时辰。 你们为天经和拜功而早起吧! 它为你们的其余的日子定下调子。
articles.title_zh: 当早晨与虔诚混淆时
articles.content: “Do your quiet time with God every morning.” “Give God your first hours (your best hours!) of the day.” “Rise early for Scripture and prayer; it sets the tone for the rest of your day!” From pulpits to podcasts, I’ve heard these sentiments often in Christian circles. The instructions aren’t just to spend alone time with God but to specifically do so as the very first act of your day. For many, the “morning quiet time” has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. Actor Mark Wahlberg once went viral on Instagram for a screenshot of his morning routine : waking up at 2:30 a.m., praying at 2:45, and completing his first workout before 5:30. This is one of many examples of how early rising has become associated with aspirational godliness. But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl? What If You Have to Sleep In? Behind the modern mindset of hyperidealized mornings is the assumption that being a “morning person” is a virtue in and of itself—a gritty choice toward wellness and productivity within everyone’s power. The implication is that if you’re disciplined and wise, you’ll set the alarm clock and start the day early; you’ll make it happen. If you’re slothful or foolish, you won’t. Extenuating circumstances are just excuses. For many, the ‘morning quiet time’ has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. But what would this mean for nurses whose work begins and ends when it’s dark outside? What about parents with newborns, whose babies’ demands don’t abide by our ideal rhythms? How about Christians who are naturally night owls: most alert, focused, and productive at night? Should these folks just suck it up and aspire to get up earlier in spite of their circumstances? Or could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical? God Loves Early Risers At first glance, it might seem that God’s Word does value our mornings most. Pastor David Mathis wrote an insightful article summarizing the abundance of instances in Scripture in which God’s people (including Christ himself!) either rose early to good effect or were directed by God to do so. Consider the Psalms: In Psalm 5:3, David says, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.” In Psalm 88:13, the Sons of Korah sing, “In the morning my prayer comes before you.” In Psalm 90:14, Moses prays to God, “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.” God clearly meets with his people in the morning. Case closed? Not quite. When you consult the whole counsel of Scripture, it becomes clear that God emphasizes meditating on his Word, singing his praises, and praying to his name just as much in the night as in the morning. Nocturnal Worship Let’s explore some nighttime examples. In Acts 16:25–26, after Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi, God’s Word notably mentions the timing of their worship: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God . . .” Silas and Paul don’t try to go to sleep early so they can engage with God at the crack of dawn. They stay up late, worshiping at midnight. The results are profound. In Psalm 63:5–6, David prays to the Lord, “My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.” This psalm as a whole is arguably a nighttime prayer. David prays these lyrics to the Lord seemingly all while on his “bed,” singing midnight praises. Consider Jesus’s earthly life. On the fateful day before his crucifixion, when it comes to spending devoted time alone with his Father, Jesus prays passionately, in Gethsemane, at night (Matt. 26:36–56). There is no mention in the Gospels of Jesus rising early on this momentous day; it might have happened, but the recorded emphasis is Jesus’s spiritual devotion in the dark. Morning and evening aren’t pitted against each other in the Bible. They’re a complementary pair: Psalm 77:2 says, “In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying.” Psalm 88:1 says, “O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.” Psalm 92:1–2 says, “It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night.” What does this mean for practical living? If you’ve never tried it, consider adding nighttime worship to your spiritual toolbox. Carve out time to pray, praise, and ponder the Scriptures before bed. If you struggle with insomnia, see it as a devotional opportunity. If your brain just won’t turn off at 3:00 a.m., fellowship with your Maker rather than letting your mind wander aimlessly. In a unique season of spiritual desperation, set your alarm clock for the middle of the night, to wait on the Lord under the stars, to intently watch for his presence and answers to prayer (Ps. 130:6). Dreams can be God’s chosen instrument to instruct and encourage his people (e.g., Gen. 28:10–22; 37:6–7; 1 Kings 3:5; Matt. 1:20–21; 2:13; Acts 2:17). Dreams appear in Scripture as a meaningful spiritual realm, and the thoughts you think in the final moments before sleep often seep into your nightly imagination. What better way to end your day than to fill your mind with God and his excellencies, to draw your heart near to his love, and to pray for spiritual protection while you slumber. Ultimately, if mornings are a perpetual struggle for you, release yourself from the guilt and legalism of needing to give God a half hour every morning. Give him your nights! Balanced Worship If you’ve found it fruitful to rise early to devote alone time to God, continue doing so with discipline and joy. But beware of imposing your own daily spiritual practices on others with a prideful narrow-mindedness that Scripture lacks. Release yourself from the guilt and legalism of needing to give God a half hour every morning. Give him your nights! Excessive sleeping can be a sign of sinful sloth (Prov. 19:15). But biblically, the godly Christian can please God just as much staying up late to worship as rising early. Both routes are biblical and blessed. The mature Christian life, across different seasons, will have various rhythms of dedicated worship at all times of the day and night: sometimes at the crack of dawn, other times at noon, or even in the dark (Deut. 6:4–7). Sacrifice your mornings to the Lord when you’re able. Devote your evenings too.

你们应当在早晨和真主在一起享受。 你们应当在白昼中为真主创造最初的时辰。 你们为天经和拜功而早起吧!它为你们的其余的日子定下调子。 我经常在基督教圈子里听到这些情绪, 这些指示不仅仅是与上帝单独相处,
对许多人来说,“早晨的宁静时间”已经成为衡量你与上帝关系如何的尺度。 演员Mark Wahlberg曾经在Instagram上进行病毒传播, 这是许多例子之一,说明早起如何与渴望的虔诚联系在一起。
但做个早起的人 比做个夜猫子好吗? 如果你必须睡觉呢? 现代思想认为, " 晨光人 " 本身就是一种美德 -- -- 在每个人的权力范围内对健康和生产力的粗暴选择。
也就是说,如果你有纪律和智慧,你会设置警报钟,并提前开工;你会让它实现。 如果你懒惰或愚蠢, 减轻罪责只是借口 对许多人来说,`早晨的平静时间'已成为衡量你与上帝关系如何的尺度。
这对护士来说意味着什么? 父母若有新生儿, 基督教徒自然是夜猫子, 这些人是否应该吸起来 渴望早起 不顾自己的处境?
或者说,我们理想化的清晨宁静时期,是否比圣经更具有文化色彩? 上帝爱早起者 乍一看,上帝的言语似乎对我们的早晨最为重要。
大卫·马西斯牧师写了一篇深刻的文章,总结了圣经中大量的例子,其中上帝的百姓(包括基督本人)不是早起,就是奉上帝的指示这样做。
你看看《古兰经》。在《古兰经》5:3中,大卫说:耶和华啊!你在早晨听见我的声音。 在"诗经"第88卷第13节中,可拉之子们唱道:"早晨,我的祈祷降临你们面前。 在《诗经》第90章第14节中,穆萨祈祷真主说:你们以你们的坚忍的爱,在早晨拯救我们,以便我们快乐和快乐。 早晨,上帝显然与他的族人相会。 结案? 没有
当你参考整个天经的教诲时,显然上帝强调冥想他的言语,歌颂他的赞美,在黑夜和早晨一样祈祷他的名字. 夜礼拜 让我们来探索一些夜间的例子。
在16:25-26号法案中,保罗和西拉斯被囚禁在菲利皮之后,上帝的言语特别提到了他们的崇拜时间:"大约午夜保罗和西拉斯在向上帝祈祷和歌颂. Silas和Paul不会早睡, 他们熬夜,午夜礼拜 其结果是深刻的。
在"诗经"卷63:5-6中,大卫向主祈祷说:"我的灵魂将满足于肥美的食物,我的嘴将喜悦地赞颂你,当我想起你在我的床上,并在黑夜的表里思念你。 这整个诗歌可以说是夜祷. 大卫在他“床上”唱午夜赞美时,
想想耶稣的地球生活。 在他被钉十字架的前一天,在与父亲单独度过时间的时候,耶稣在夜里热切地祈祷在Gethsemane(Matt. 26:36-56). 福音书中没有提到耶稣在这个重要的日子提前升起;它可能已经发生,但记录的强调是耶稣在黑暗中的精神奉献.
早晚并不在圣经中相互对立。 他们是一个互补的对:诗篇77:2说,“在我麻烦的一天里,我寻求主;在夜晚,我的手被伸开而不磨损。” "诗经"第88卷第1节说:"耶和华啊!我的救赎之神啊!我昼夜在你们面前呐喊。 诗篇92: 1–2说: " 向耶和华致谢,赞颂你的名字是件好事,至尊者啊!
在早晨和晚上,你应当说出你坚定的情谊。 这对实际生活意味着什么? 若你从未尝试过, 刻意祈祷、赞美、在睡觉前思索天经。 如果你与失眠作斗争, 把它视为一个奉献的机会。
如果你的大脑不会在凌晨3点关闭, 在一个独特的精神绝望的季节,将你的闹钟定在半夜,在星辰下等待主,有意地看着他的出现和对祈祷的回答(Ps130:6).
梦可以是上帝选择用来指示和鼓励其人民的工具(例如:Gen. 28:10–22;37:6–7;1 Kings 3:5;Matt. 1:20–21;2:13;Act 2:17). 梦境在圣经中作为一个有意义的精神领域出现,在睡眠前的最后时刻你所想的思想常常渗入你的夜梦中.
结束你的一天比用上帝和他卓越的神灵 让你的心接近他的爱 以及趁你睡着时祈祷精神保护更好的方法 归根结底,如果早晨对你来说是永恒的挣扎,那么就从每天早上需要给上帝一个半小时的内疚和法律主义中解放出来. 给他你的夜晚!
平衡礼拜 如果你发现早起为上帝奉献时间, 但当心将自己的日常精神实践 强加于别人 以骄傲的狭隘的思想, 而圣经缺乏。 让自己摆脱每天早上需要给上帝半小时的内疚和法律主义. 给他你的夜晚!
过度睡眠可能代表罪恶的懒惰(19:15,普罗夫)。 但圣经上,虔诚的基督教徒可以取悦上帝 就像早起一样 晚起崇拜 这两条路线都是圣经性的和吉祥的.
成熟的基督教生活,跨越不同的季节,在白天和夜晚的任何时候都会有各种献身崇拜的节奏:有时在黎明的裂缝,其他时候在中午,甚至黑暗中(德国6:4-7). 尽你所能为主牺牲早晨。 将你的夜晚也。

articles.summary_zh: 不久前,我儿子问我 大卫国王在塞缪尔8号杀死的所有人 我们一直读那本书, 他有权被打扰。 因此,我们讨论了为什么他不紧张,我们如何发展道德本能,以及我们如何回应因旧约中这些和类似说法而拒绝上帝的人。 我们一起做杂耍 我将指向我的朋友Gavin Ortlund的YouTube频道, 然后,几年后,我将指给他看加文的书,包括他的最新著作,《基督教为什么讲道理:关于耶稣的书》、《世界的谜》和《你心中的长寿》。
articles.title_zh: 基督教有意义吗？论上帝、邪恶和痛苦（与Gavin Ortlund合作）
articles.content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. In This Episode 00:00 – Why people may be more open to spiritual answers today 03:36 – “The ache” and the longing for transcendence 09:29 – What about Christianity makes the least sense to Gavin? 11:39 – The problem of evil and the limits of tidy answers 19:09 – The growing challenge of divine hiddenness 24:34 – Fine-tuning and the odds of a life-permitting universe 32:07 – Is morality without God just a matter of taste? 37:25 – Slavery, the Bible, and the Christian roots of human equality 42:23 – Why fulfilled prophecy surprised Gavin 48:00 – What apologetic questions should Christians prepare for next? Resources Mentioned: Why Christianity Makes Sense by Gavin Ortlund Mere Christianity by C. S. Lewis Making Sense of God by Timothy Keller The Reason for God by Timothy Keller The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky Bullies and Saints by John Dickson Dominion by Tom Holland Gavin Ortlund’s YouTube channel, “ Truth Unites “ The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics SIGN UP for my newsletter, Unseen Things . Help The Gospel Coalition renew and unify the contemporary church in the ancient gospel: Donate today . articles.title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
articles.summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
articles.summary_zh: 2016年至2018年,任社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在脸书和推特上, 如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到 我成长在一个保守的基督教家庭 在郊区, 或者我每天的教育, 从4岁开始,在基督教学校。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度.
articles.title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
articles.content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). This gospel of the kingdom must be lived out through embodied action. Mapping Our Approaches to Cross and Kingdom Most Christians today rightly see these two gospel aspects—the message proper and its kingdom implications—as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. As a result, many emphasize only one aspect or the other. And sadly, some neglect both these aspects of the gospel altogether. Nicholas Wolterstorff writes that shalom is “a harmony and delight in all of one’s relationships: between us and God, us and other people, us and other cultures, us and creation, and between us and our very selves.” In the four-quadrant grid below, I’ve mapped out the ways we typically approach the cross and kingdom aspects of the gospel. (For more, see section II.3 of The Gospel Coalition’s Theological Vision for Ministry .) Christ’s sacrifice on the cross restores us to harmony and delight with God. This is our most important relationship, and it’s represented on the diagram by the upward-pointing vertical axis. A kingdom emphasis on harmony and delight in other people, other cultures, and the creation is represented by the rightward-pointing horizontal axis. Quadrants II and IV represent two errors—the false choice of emphasizing either the cross or kingdom while neglecting the other. Many American Christians have been ensnared by one of these two quadrants. Quadrant III designates a total neglect of both cross and also kingdom. All these disconnects result from misunderstanding who a Christian is and what a Christian should do in this broken world. Quadrant IV: Individualized Gospel Advocates of an individualized gospel (quadrant IV) want to get people saved for the afterlife without stressing the social implications for this life. When sinners are saved, we always celebrate! However, Christians who fit in this quadrant often don’t emphasize the kingdom aspect of the gospel. Such individuals and churches may financially support ministries in underresourced neighborhoods but don’t often emphasize transformative service there. Many such churches and their members may not understand or appreciate the depth and range of problems in struggling communities, even in neighborhoods not far from them. Quadrant II: Social Gospel Advocates of the social gospel seek to meet people’s imminent needs but neglect their ultimate need of the salvation Jesus offers. This is a scandalous compromise, and it’s the false gospel I believed for nearly a decade and then proclaimed as a social media justice warrior. My wife and I moved into our underresourced neighborhood to live close to the school where I served for 18 years. Living and working among the poor showed me that many people need more than hearing about Jesus alone. They needed tangible help. Many of my quadrant IV friends concluded my neighbors were ignorant, dangerous, and to be avoided. So I reacted to my peers by propelling myself into the social gospel. Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. The social gospel is an late 19th- and early 20th-century theological movement focused on breaking the chains of oppression and championing the poor. Advocates seek to make Christ’s kingdom manifest on earth through acts of charity, philanthropy, and just legislation. Some social-gospel advocates choose to live close to the poor to improve their neighborhoods and lives. Yet the social gospel focuses solely on meeting imminent needs. It neglects preaching Christ as the sinner’s Savior. In fact, many social-gospel advocates reject the evangelical gospel and biblical authority. Many parachurch organizations that serve underresourced communities are held hostage by social-gospel theology. Though the leaders may be Christians, you can scour the organizations’ websites and messaging yet find no evidence of an orthodox theological foundation. Quadrant III: Faux Gospel Those who ignore both the gospel of the cross and the gospel of th

2016年至2018年,任社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在脸书和推特上,
如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到 我成长在一个保守的基督教家庭 在郊区, 或者我每天的教育, 从4岁开始,在基督教学校。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.
然而,这个以福音为导向的我青年世界被故意洗涤,并在仅仅10分钟之内就脱离了贫困和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距时,我成了在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我的成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.
自2001年起, 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教堂里有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻里之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。
所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。
我开始看到圣经福音书中的两个方面。 让我们把他们称为十字架的福音和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救和接纳信徒作为自己的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 在罪恶中,我们是他的敌人。
在基督中,我们相信好消息,我们与上帝和解(5:6-10室),并保证与上帝永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写的那样,“基督也曾因罪恶而受苦,善人因不义者而受苦,以便他把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。
此外,福音的交叉方面强调,受委托传达这一信息的人必须与一个迷失和垂死的世界分享(Matt. 28:18-20)。 十字架的福音必须预告;必须宣布。 这是优先事项。 从这个福音中流传着每一个好礼物.
我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。 王国的福音是好消息,上帝对正义、善良与和平的意志已经释放。 作为上帝的子孙,信徒们被邀请在确保王国使命取得成果方面发挥作用。
耶稣在部里首先发出一个信息,宣称“向穷人提供好消息”和“向......受压迫的人提供自由”(公爵4:18)。 他呼吁他的听众悔过自新, 他特别斥责法利赛人忽视“较重要的法律事项:正义、慈悲和忠诚”(23:23)。
保罗也教导道,福音不仅使我们与上帝团聚,而且通过在教堂中调和分裂的人民来伸张正义。 他写道,“[基督]自己是我们的和平,他使我们两个[种族群 都成了和平,并用他的肉体打破了敌对的分隔墙”(Eph 2:14)。
我们履行法律,通过我们作为立法者的身份,活出福音的王国影响(马特:9)。 福音的王国方面为我们提供了追求上帝的旨意的愿景,即 " 在地上像在天上一样 " (6:10),即看到一切事物都变得新(Rev.21:5)。 这个王国的福音 必须通过体现的行动得以实现
今天大多数基督徒正确地将这两个福音方面——即信息本身及其对王国的影响——视为同一圣经派的一部分。 但我们往往不认为它们必然相互交织。 因此,许多人只强调某一方面。 不幸的是,有些人完全忽略了福音的这两个方面。
尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫(Nicholas Wolterstorff)写道, Shalom是“我们和上帝、我们和其他人、我们和其他文化、我们和创造,以及我们和我们自己之间的和谐与快乐。 ” 在下面的四方网格中, 我绘制了我们一般如何处理福音的十字和王国方面。
(详见福音联盟的神学展望第二.3节。 ) 基督在十字架上的牺牲使我们恢复了与上帝的和谐与喜悦。 这是我们最重要的关系,它用向上的垂直轴在图上代表。
一个王国在他人,其他文化中强调和谐与快乐,而创造者则以右倾的横向轴线为代表. 四方二和四代表两个错误——错误的选择是强调十字架或王国,而忽略另一个。 许多美国基督徒被这两个四角星中的一个所迷惑.
四方三指完全忽视十字架和王国. 所有这些脱节都是由于误解基督徒是谁,基督徒在这个破碎的世界中应该做什么. Quadrant IV:一个个性化福音(quadrant IV)的个性化福音代言人希望让人们为来世而得到救赎,而不要强调对今世生活的社会影响.
罪人获救后,我们总是庆祝! 基督教徒通常不强调福音的王国方面。 这些个人和教会可能会在资金不足的街区里为各部提供财政支持,
许多这类教会及其成员可能不了解或理解在艰难的社区中,甚至在离他们不远的街区中,问题的严重性和范围。 四方二:社会福音书. 社会福音的倡导者试图满足人们的迫切需求,但忽略了他们对耶稣所提供的救赎的最终需求。
这也是我近十年来所相信的虚假福音, 我妻子和我搬到我们资源不足的街区 住在我工作18年的学校附近 在穷人中生活和工作表明,许多人需要的不只是听到耶稣的孤独. 他们需要实际帮助。
我的许多四象限朋友认为,我的邻居是无知的,危险的,需要避免。 所以我对同龄人的反应是 推动自己进入社会福音。 今天大多数基督徒将这两个福音方面视为同一个圣经派的一部分. 但我们往往不认为它们必然相互交织。
社会福音是19世纪晚期和20世纪早期的神学运动,其重点是打破压迫的枷锁,拥护穷人. 通过慈善、慈善和公正立法, 一些社会神道倡导者选择住在穷人身边以改善他们的邻居和生活.
然而,社会福音仅仅侧重于满足紧迫的需要。 它忽略了宣扬基督是罪人的救世主. 事实上,许多社会-神道倡导者拒绝福音和圣经权威. 许多为资源不足的社区服务的教会组织被社会神学所牵制。
虽然领导者可能是基督徒,但你们可以搜索各组织的网站和消息,但没有找到正统神学基础的证据。 四方三:福州福音 那些无视十字架福音和福音的人

articles.title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
articles.summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
articles.summary_zh: “我从来不担心像希特勒这样的人。 ” 这并非一个疯子或一个有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些话来自一位牧师, 他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁, 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰; 就在第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 被安置在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂做助理牧师 他将在接下来的30年里忠实地传教。
articles.title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
articles.content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. Throughout the church’s history, we’ve often turned to national politics. In a talk titled “ Living in Revolutionary Times ,” Lloyd-Jones rebukes the evangelicals of his day, who “seem to think that they are innovators in saying that we should all be taking an interest in politics and social matters.” But this is nothing new. Lloyd-Jones recalls, “They do not seem to have heard of the ‘social gospel’ craze of the earlier part of this century. All this has been tried with great thoroughness.” A preacher unaware of the dangerous pitfalls the church has already fallen into is sure to lead his congregation into one of those pits. This was the great danger, in Lloyd-Jones’s mind, of harnessing power for the church through political means. Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In that same talk, Lloyd-Jones cautions preachers against the temptation to quickly gather a crowd by preaching politics. His words feel even more timely today: I well remember certain men who were concerned about social and political matters, and who constantly preached on such themes, and packed their chapels for a while, but only as long as they preached politics. The moment they began to preach the gospel truly the crowds left them. Politically-minded people are always ready to make use of the church, but they always abandon and shun her when she ceases to be of any value to them. American pulpits have been infected with this kind of partisan preaching for decades now, on both the left and right. It draws crowds but does a disservice to the gospel. It’s important for Christians to offer a robust political and social ethic, but not at the expense of the gospel. The former flows from the latter, and the order is irreversible. Remember the ‘Leaven’ For Lloyd-Jones, spiritual resurrection—not political revolution—would save the world. The church didn’t need a theology of liberation but a theology of “leaven.” Drawing a straight line through the New Testament, he says , “The Christian is represented as ‘salt’ in society and ‘leaven,’ and surely the whole point of those comparisons is that Christian influence is to be a quiet influence and a slow process of influencing society.” Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In times of political crisis, such as our own, we’re tempted to forget this basic biblical principle. We must remember that “the kingdom of God is like leaven” (Matt. 13:33). If we’re to have social and political influence, it’ll only happen through preaching and preserving the gospel, so that regenerate Christians can be salt and light in the public square. On May 21, 1943, when Westminster Chapel was finally seeing signs of stability after the bombings, Lloyd-Jones wrote a letter responding to a congregant who was thanking him for his faithful preaching. He ended by saying , “The supreme need of the hour is intense prayer for spiritual revival on the part of Christian people.” The Doctor was interested in treating the disease, not the symptoms. That’s why he could speak with such audacity, testifying that he was “never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” As wicked as Hitler was, he was merely symptomatic of the spiritual disease of the human heart—to which the gospel alone is the cure.
articles.content_zh:
“我从来不担心像希特勒这样的人。” 这并非一个疯子或一个有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些话来自一位牧师, 他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁, 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
就在第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 被安置在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂做助理牧师 他将在接下来的30年里忠实地传教。 传教士攻下弹坑一年后,希特勒开始对伦敦的轰炸战役. 在该地区约700座教堂中,有624座被炸毁,91座被完全摧毁。
令人惊讶的是,威斯敏斯特礼拜堂(Westminster Chapel)作为当时伦敦最大的教堂之一,并没有在轰炸闪电中被摧毁。 Iain Murray在其关于劳埃德-琼斯的经典传记中写道,
炸弹震动了整个建筑,石膏和灰尘落在会众身上,包括劳埃德-琼斯的“医生”身上。 在暂停之后,劳埃德-琼斯只是继续了他的祈祷,礼拜活动畅通无阻. Lloyd -Jones为我们的政治焦虑时期 提供了必要的纠正 一些基督徒诉诸于绝望,而另一些则试图革命.
我们需要的是政治神学 当炸弹爆炸时它仍然宣扬基督 以下是在政治危机时期我们可以从劳埃德-琼斯部学到的三个教训。 拒绝索尔的盔甲,当英格兰显然正在进入战争时,劳埃德-琼斯将他的妻子和他们的两个孩子送回威尔士,并离开这座城市,不知结果如何.
在与他妻子的简短和紧急的通信中,他写道:"离开你和我,以及上帝手中的一切,你会得到安宁和安息。 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂中许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷. 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂中许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷.
由于恐惧和恐慌,许多人开始放弃教会的武器,代之以国家的武器. 但劳埃德-琼斯拒绝模糊界限.
当战争处于最糟糕的状态,他的集会由于死亡和流离失所而减少到极少数时,他仍然坚决申明2科林斯人10:4:“我们战争的武器不是肉体的,而是通过上帝而强大的力量来拉倒坚固的阵地”(KJV)。
劳埃德-琼斯拒绝让革命联盟和战术渗透到教会中:唉,教会经常试图用类似武器来对付世界及其迫害敌人者的力量. 她与国家结盟,并试图在物质上加强自己。
她一直缓慢地发现大卫很久以前在与高丽的战斗中发现的东西,即她不能在索尔的盔甲中作战,而必须永远使用自己熟悉的,本意使用的武器.
劳埃德-琼斯在索尔的军械库里看到了相似之处, 与大卫的悲哀一样,祈祷可能出现在世界的眼中,令人悲哀的是,反对法西斯主义的武器不足。 但上帝的武器比人的武器还大
拒绝Lloyd-Jones派福音书, 认为当恐惧笼罩人民时, 教会特别容易受到政治偶像崇拜。 与在戈利亚斯面前摇晃的以色列人一样,我们常常感到唯一合理的反应是找到我们自己的“强人”来战斗。 在教会历史上,我们经常转向国家政治。
在一篇题为“生活在革命时报”的演讲中,劳埃德-琼斯斥责了当时的福音派教徒,他们“似乎认为他们只是说我们大家都应该关心政治和社会事务的创新者。 但这不是什么新鲜事。 Lloyd-Jones回忆说, " 他们似乎没有听说过本世纪早期的`社会福音'狂热。
所有这一切都经过了非常彻底的尝试。” 一个牧师不知道教堂已经陷入了危险的陷阱 肯定会把他的会众带到其中的一个坑里 劳埃德-琼斯认为,这是通过政治手段为教会掌握权力的巨大危险。
任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论, 在同一话中,劳埃德-琼斯告诫传教士们不要受到通过宣扬政治来迅速聚集人群的诱惑.
他的言语今天感觉更加及时:我清楚地记得某些关心社会和政治事务的人,他们不断宣扬这种主题,打包了一段时间的礼拜堂,但只要他们宣扬政治. 当他们开始宣扬福音的时候, 人群真的离开了他们。
政治思想的人总是准备利用教堂,但当她不再对他们有任何价值时,他们总是抛弃和避开她. 几十年来,美国纸币 一直感染这种党派传教 左右两侧。 它吸引了人群,但不利于福音。
基督教徒必须提供强有力的政治和社会道德, 前者从后者流出,顺序不可逆. 记住劳埃德-琼斯的“遗言 ” ( Leaven),
教会并不需要解放神学,而需要“离开”神学。 在新约中画一条直线,他说 : “ 基督徒在社会中被代表为`盐'和`离开',这些比较的全部要点无疑是,基督教的影响是静静的,是影响社会的缓慢过程。 任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论
或要求国家基督教化, 在政治危机时期,比如我们自己的时代,我们想忘记这个基本的圣经原则。 我们必须记住,“上帝的王国就像离开的”(Matt. 13:33)。
要想有社会和政治影响,这只能通过传教和维护福音来发生,这样再生基督徒就可以在公共广场上成为盐和光。 1943年5月21日,当威斯敏斯特礼拜堂终于在爆炸发生后看到稳定的迹象时,劳埃德-琼斯写了一封信,答复了一位正在感谢他忠实传教的教友.
他最后说,“这一时刻的最高需要是基督教人民为精神复兴而强烈祈祷。” 医生对治疗疾病感兴趣,而不是症状。
这就是为什么他可以如此大胆地说话,证明他“从来不担心像希特勒这样的人。 ” 与希特勒一样邪恶,他只是人类心灵精神疾病的症状——只有福音才能治愈。

articles.title: Can’t You Just Love Everyone?
articles.summary: “Love one another.” This is one of the undeniable imperatives of Christianity. God is love (1 John 4:8, 16). We must love one another (1 John 4:11). By this love all men know that we are Christ’s disciples (John 13:35). Love fulfills the law (Romans 13:10). So why not just love one another? Why build walls, make distinctions, establish boundaries, and draw lines? Why confront sins? Why not welcome all equally?  Can ’ t you just love everyone?   The impulse and the argument “just to love everyone

articles.content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very important king or queen inside”; those guards, he contends, are our habits, and “the strength of the soldiers determines how protected the palace is” (158). Early in the book, James calls teens to learn discernment. As he unpacks this habit, he warns them away from the siren song of social media influencers who question parental authority: “When an online influencer who doesn’t know you or care for you speaks about your parents or mentors in a way that makes you want to trust those people less and the influencer more, that’s a massive sign that what you’re listening to is false” (44). Yet James doesn’t merely tell young people to flee digital technology’s dangers; he also beckons them to put on habits that will help them cultivate virtue, in-person friendship, accountability, industrious work, creativity, and rest. For Parents Too Many of these habits are relational. In his introduction, for example, James encourages teens to read his book with a parent, teacher, pastor, or mentor. The discussion questions he includes at the end of each chapter make this counsel practical. This counsel is also wise, because while Scroll Less, Live More is a book for teens, it’s a book for parents too. As a parent and youth worker, I found James’s encouragement to develop a habit of self-awareness convicting. He calls readers to pay attention when being online leads to feelings of anger, anxiety, or boredom so that you know when to “log off and touch grass.” Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia : “Spiritual laziness that causes you to fill up on meaningless things so much that you cannot delight in God” (65). He nailed me. How many times do I fill life’s quiet moments—waiting in a line, a few minutes between meetings, or sadly even lulls in conversation—by pulling out my phone instead of being attentive to nature, the people around me, and the Lord? Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia . I can get frustrated when I see this tendency in teens, but as Brett McCracken writes , “What parents model with our own devices ultimately matters more than what we say to our kids about them.” James’s book helped me see ways I’ve failed to fight endless scrolling in my own life. As parents, we need God’s Spirit to help us grow in self-awareness about our tech habits. We need his grace to help us confess those failures to the teens we parent and lead. And we need a heart of wisdom and phone-stack intentionality, not just at youth group meetings but throughout our lives. Scroll Less, Live More helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.

每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。
我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。 这帮助了我们团体的学生更密切地关注彼此和圣经文本。 在他实用的新书"Scroll Less"(Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Health Tech Habits for Teens)中,塞缪尔·詹姆斯称赞了一些类似的做法.
他的目标是让青少年 " 生动地了解在当今数字时代将[圣经上 智慧应用于技术应用的外表 " (155)。 詹姆斯认识到简单、可重复的做法可以帮助年轻人抵制当今技术推广的愚蠢,让他们在上帝的恐惧中成长。
Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More 在他的前作中为成年人奠定的基础上, 科技并非中立。 而是一股强大的力量, “塑造并影响我们,
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 为了说明这个事实,詹姆斯指出19世纪发明的技术: 在电话之前, 人们刚刚接受, 如果他们不和别人在同一间屋子里,
在电话引入后,能够随时与另一个地方的某个人通信不仅成为可能,而且非常重要.
(125) 同样地,21世纪的技术,如基因人工智能,也带来了新的可能性和更大的期望: " 人工智能在人类很少直接参与的情况下生产出惊人的作品和艺术的能力,使人们期望经常用于这些目的是正常的 " (127)。 我们越是放弃我们的创造力和努力,我们就越相信我们应该这样做。
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 数字技术也以其他方式改变我们。 James借鉴了Neil Postman、Nicholas Carr、Marshall McLuhan等科技现实主义者的作品, 詹姆斯反复地向年轻人展示,不良的数字习惯如何影响他们的认知,情感和关系.
生活在电话里会减缓思考, 让青少年感到焦虑甚至愤怒, 智慧之道:守护你的心 我们如何帮助年轻人避免这条道路? 詹姆斯给青少年一些实际的鼓励,让他们在一夜之间在卧室以外的地方充电电话.
他还提供了一份自查问题清单,帮助他们提高自我意识,他呼吁遵守家庭规则,例如只在家庭的空地使用装置。 但最终,詹姆斯相信,使用良好的技术不仅仅涉及遵循一个做和不做的清单。
他写道, 我们不需要一连串的规则, 每次苹果公司发布新手机或新社交媒体应用时, 我们需要智慧。 (16-17) 普罗活佛说:"对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,对圣者的知识是洞察力"(9:10).
詹姆斯明白,智慧和上帝的知识的不断增长,不仅需要调整一个人的屏幕时间设置,还需要守护一个人的心。 詹姆斯鼓励青少年将心想成一个国王或女王所居住的宫殿. 他说,“在任何皇家宫殿里,你肯定能找到士兵来监视谁和什么人可以接触到里面非常重要的国王或女王”;
他认为,这些警卫是我们的习惯,“士兵的力量决定了宫殿的保护程度”(158)。 在书的早期,詹姆斯召集少年来学习辨识.
当他解开这种习惯时,他警告他们不要听那些质疑父母权威的社交媒体影响者所唱的警笛:“当一个不了解你或关心你的网络影响者以一种方式谈论你的父母或导师,使你更希望信任这些人,而影响者更多,这是你所听到的都是虚假的大规模迹象”(44)。
但詹姆斯并不只是告诉年轻人逃离数字技术的危险;他还诱使他们树立习惯,帮助他们培养美德、亲身友谊、责任感、勤奋的工作、创造力和休息。 对于父母来说,这些习惯中有许多是相互关联的。
例如,在介绍中,詹姆斯鼓励青少年与家长,教师,牧师,或导师一起阅读他的书. 他在每个章节结尾处包括的讨论问题使该律师成为实际。 这本书也是明智的, 因为虽然《Less Scroll》,
作为父母和青年工作者,我发现詹姆斯鼓励培养一种自我认识定罪的习惯。
他呼吁读者关注网络引发愤怒、焦虑或无聊的感觉, Listless boorom是Acedia罪的一种形式:“导致你充斥无意义的事物而不能对上帝取悦的原始懒惰”(65)。 他钉住我。
我有多少次在静静的瞬间, 等待一行, 几分钟的会面, 无名无姓的无聊是阿塞迪亚罪的一种形式
但正如Brett McCracken所写 的 , “ 父母用我们自己的设备建模最终比我们对孩子说的更重要。 ” 詹姆士的书帮助我看到了自己一生中一直未能与无尽的卷轴斗争的方式。 作为父母,我们需要上帝的精神来帮助我们增强对技术习惯的自我意识。
我们需要他的恩典来帮助我们 向那些我们父母和领导的孩子承认这些失败 我们需要一个智慧的心脏 和电话袋的故意, 不仅在青年小组会议上,而且我们一生。 Scroll Less, Live More帮助青少年和家长发展他们所需要的技术技能,以过着根植于现实并充满智慧的生活.

articles.title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
articles.content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. Adherents have a sense of higher purpose and calling as they’re suddenly confronted with extraordinary individual wealth and wrestle with the consequences of their technological discoveries. It’s hard to describe effective altruism without addressing its more eccentric views, some of which divide the movement itself. For example, the focus on animal welfare has led many in the movement to believe that any and all sentient beings share the same moral value, including but not limited to shrimp . Yes, since a dollar can go a long way to protect the well-being of a single crustacean , this cause could be the most efficient use of charitable giving. Notably, the effective altruist community has also drawn scrutiny for its sexual culture. A 2023 Time investigation highlighted how the movement’s overwhelmingly male membership, heavy overlap between work and home life, and its subculture of polyamory (which some have promoted as more rational than monogamy) has created a “culture of sexual harassment and abuse.” These dynamics have caused many—including Christians—to be concerned about the group’s outsize influence on culture. What Effective Altruism Promises (and Fails to Deliver) Effective altruism’s turn toward longtermism promises that the right people, armed with the right understanding of the stakes, can steer humanity safely through an uncertain future. Many in this community believe their adherence to consequentialism and longtermism gives them a special moral qualification to shape public policy. In their own eyes, effective altruists are the men and women of the hour. This conviction has moved from theory into practice. Political engagement by adherents has increased both on the public stage and backstage through building and funding civil society institutions to influence policymakers to embrace their ideology. One of the movement’s most prominent figures (though he has denied belonging to it), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, has been leaning on this philosophy to guide his leadership of his company and shape his approach to the future of AI . Yet for all its ambition, the movement struggles to deliver on what it promises. Effective altruism’s confidence in its own reasoning to navigate the future is a hubristic claim to possess unprecedented human knowledge. Any ethic that judges right and wrong by outcomes assumes we can reliably know what our actions will produce. It treats the future as a closed system of causes and effects that the right person or algorithm can calculate. But human knowledge is finite. We can’t trace the full effects of a single choice, much less forecast the welfare of billions of potential lives. At best, an outcome-based ethic can render its moral verdict only in hindsight. Most fundamentally, effective altruism fails us because it’s an ethic without a moral foundation. It has a laudable premise: Too many people around the globe are suffering, and those with means should help. Adherents can accurately quantify certain societal woes and calculate which actions could most efficiently produce the greatest benefit. But the philosophy largely assumes the moral obligations on which those calculations depend. In Singer’s foundational essay, he uses an illustration of a man wearing expensive sneakers who walks past a drowning child. He does a moral calculation that it’s better to save the child even if it ruins his shoes. The illustration works only because we already know the child matters and that walking past would be monstrous. But a strictly consequentialist framework can’t tell us why . If people are ultimately containers of welfare to be added up, then no one has worth in himself. Each matters only as a quantity in a calculation. And who decides which quantities count? Without an external source of moral truth, the answer is ultimately the individual. Each effective altruist must reason his way to his own conclusion about what “the most good” is, and no authority outside himself can tell him he’s wrong. Taken to its logical end, this leaves room for almost anything

过去十年来,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷扎根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是因为它的想法决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。
《经济学家》最近将哲学称为“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称该运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。
作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能实现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音是不一致的,并且是一个糟糕的替代物。 什么是有效的异端主义?
有效的利他主义在2000年代末和2010年代初从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和基于证据的慈善运动的趋同中出现.
澳大利亚学者Peter Singer以他1972年的论文“饥荒、富裕和道德”为重要基础,他认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务。 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。
有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥他们在社会中的优势。
有效替代主义中心解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥他们在社会中的优势。
这场运动随着多个慈善组织的成立而成形, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“影响大”的职业。
他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球健康、动物福利和经济差距的努力。
在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后代和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期未来是我们时代的关键道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的人应该得到平衡的权衡——而且可能有数万亿。
许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来防范风险, 即使这让今天的美好事业饿死, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下一个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能。
对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对潜在的AI启示录的担忧解释了为何该运动在AI研究,AI公司,AI倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究者和硅谷科技流派中拥有自然的读者,
有效的利他主义使技术专家能够以能够感到熟悉的方式处理伦理问题:一系列概率、权衡和预期结果——衡量个人的道德地位作为数学计算,类似于建立软件程序的过程,不同投入导致不同的产出。
对于那些习惯于通过智慧和批判性分析来解决复杂项目的野心勃勃的个人来说,这一运动在一个常常感到孤立的行业中为社区带来安慰。 坚持者有更高的目标感, 并召唤他们突然面对非凡的个人财富,
很难描述有效的利他主义, 例如,对动物福利的重视使得运动中许多人相信,任何和所有神灵生物都具有同样的道德价值,包括但不限于虾。
是的,由于一美元对保护单一甲壳类动物的福祉可以发挥很大的作用,因此这一事业可能是慈善捐赠的最有效用途。 值得注意的是,有效的利他主义社区也对其性文化进行了审查。
2023年的一项时间调查凸显了该运动绝大多数男性成员、工作和家庭生活之间的严重重叠、以及其多元文化(有些人提倡这种文化比一夫一妻制更合理)如何创造了“性骚扰和虐待文化 ” 。 这些动态导致包括基督徒在内的许多人担心该团体对文化的影响过大。
有效的利他主义向长期主义的转变会保证,以正确理解利害关系为武装的正确人民能够安全地引导人类渡过不确定的未来。 这个社区中许多人认为,他们坚持后果主义和长期主义,使他们具有制定公共政策的特殊道德资格。
在他们自己的眼里,有效的利他主义者是时空的男女. 这种信念已经从理论转变为实践。 通过建立和资助民间社会机构影响决策者接受其意识形态,信徒们在公共舞台和后台的政治参与有所增加。
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei(虽然他否认自己属于这个运动)最知名的人物之一, 然而,运动的雄心壮志却在努力兑现它的承诺。
有效的利他主义相信它自己的通向未来的推理,是一种傲慢地宣称拥有前所未有的人类知识。 根据结果判断对错的任何道德都假定我们能够可靠地知道我们的行动将产生什么。 它把未来当作一个封闭的因果系统,由正确的人或算法来计算. 但人类的知识是有限的。
我们无法追踪单一选择的全部效果, 充其量,基于结果的伦理只有在事后才能作出道德判断。 最根本的,有效的利他主义使我们失望,因为它是一种没有道德基础的伦理。
它有一个值得称赞的前提:全球有太多的人在受苦,那些有手段的人应该提供帮助。 坚持者可以准确地量化某些社会灾难,并计算哪些行动能够最有效地产生最大的利益。 但哲学基本上承担了这些计算所依赖的道德义务。
在Singer的奠基论文中,他用一个插图说明一名穿昂贵运动鞋的人走过一个溺水的孩子. 他做了一个道德的计算,认为救孩子更好, 插图之所以有效,只是因为我们已经知道儿童的重要性,而且走过去将是可怕的。 但严格地说,
如果人们最终是福利的容器 被加起来, 那么没有人值得自己。 每种物质在计算中仅作为数量。 谁决定数量是多少? 没有道德真理的外部来源,答案最终是个人.
每一个有效的利他主义者必须解释自己对什么是“最美好”的结论, 任何外部权威都不能告诉他自己错了。 顺理成章地说,这为几乎一切留下了空间

articles.content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. articles.summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.
